clauses.title: Prohibited Conduct
clauses.body: {{companyName}} prohibits discrimination and harassment based on race, color, religion, sex, and national origin in every aspect of employment — hiring, compensation, discipline, promotion, and termination alike. Federal law makes this a legal requirement, not just a company policy choice.
clauses.gap: This specific citation covers only employers with 15 or more employees for each working day in 20 or more calendar weeks in the current or preceding year — smaller employers aren't covered by this particular statute, though state or local law may still reach them. Separately, other protected characteristics — age, disability, genetic information, and pregnancy among them — come from different federal statutes with their own coverage thresholds, not from the provision cited here.

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
citations.quote: It shall be an unlawful employment practice for an employer— (1) to fail or refuse to hire or to discharge any individual, or otherwise to discriminate against any individual with respect to his compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment, because of such individual’s race, color, religion, sex, or national origin

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(b) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Title VII, covered-employer definition
citations.quote: The term “employer” means a person engaged in an industry affecting commerce who has fifteen or more employees for each working day in each of twenty or more calendar weeks in the current or preceding calendar year

clauses.title: How to Report
clauses.body: {{employeeName}} can report suspected harassment or discrimination to a supervisor, Human Resources, or any other member of management {{employeeName}} feels comfortable approaching. A report doesn't have to follow any particular format, and {{employeeName}} isn't required to raise it with the person accused of the conduct first.

clauses.title: How the Company Responds
clauses.body: {{companyName}} will investigate reports of harassment promptly and take appropriate corrective action. This isn't just good practice — federal law gives {{companyName}} a real defense against certain harassment claims only if it can show it exercised reasonable care to prevent and promptly correct harassing behavior, and that the employee unreasonably failed to use the reporting process available.
clauses.gap: This defense has a hard limit the case establishing it is explicit about: it's only available when the harassment didn't result in a tangible employment action against the employee — a firing, demotion, undesirable reassignment, or a decision causing a significant change in benefits. If a tangible employment action occurred, the employer can't rely on this defense no matter how good its policy or response was. Separately, having a written policy like this one isn't automatically enough by itself, nor is it strictly required as a matter of law — courts look at whether the policy was actually suitable to the circumstances, not just whether one existed on paper.

citations.case: Faragher v. City of Boca Raton
citations.quote: An employer is subject to vicarious liability to a victimized employee for an actionable hostile environment created by a supervisor with immediate (or successively higher) authority over the employee. When no tangible employment action is taken, a defending employer may raise an affirmative defense to liability or damages, subject to proof by a preponderance of the evidence ... The defense comprises two necessary elements: (a) that the employer exercised reasonable care to prevent and correct promptly any sexually harassing behavior, and (b) that the plaintiff employee unreasonably failed to take advantage of any preventive or corrective opportunities provided by the employer or to avoid harm otherwise.

citations.case: Faragher v. City of Boca Raton
citations.cite: 524 U.S. 775 (1998) — on the policy itself
citations.quote: While proof that an employer had promulgated an antiharassment policy with complaint procedure is not necessary in every instance as a matter of law, the need for a stated policy suitable to the employment circumstances may appropriately be addressed in any case when litigating the first element of the defense.

citations.case: Burlington Industries, Inc. v. Ellerth
citations.cite: 524 U.S. 742 (1998) — the companion case establishing the identical defense
citations.quote: An employer is subject to vicarious liability to a victimized employee for an actionable hostile environment created by a supervisor with immediate (or successively higher) authority over the employee. When no tangible employment action is taken, a defending employer may raise an affirmative defense to liability or damages, subject to proof by a preponderance of the evidence ... The defense comprises two necessary elements: (a) that the employer exercised reasonable care to prevent and correct promptly any sexually harassing behavior, and (b) that the plaintiff employee unreasonably failed to take advantage of any preventive or corrective opportunities provided by the employer or to avoid harm otherwise.

clauses.title: No Retaliation
clauses.body: {{companyName}} will not retaliate against {{employeeName}} for reporting harassment or discrimination in good faith, participating in an investigation, or otherwise opposing conduct this policy prohibits.
clauses.gap: Retaliation under this law isn't limited to firing, demotion, or other classic employment actions — it covers anything that would materially discourage a reasonable employee from making or supporting a complaint in the first place, whether or not it affects the terms of employment itself. That's a broader standard than what counts as illegal discrimination in the first place, a distinction the statute's own text doesn't spell out but the Supreme Court has.

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-3(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Title VII, anti-retaliation provision
citations.quote: It shall be an unlawful employment practice for an employer to discriminate against any of his employees or applicants for employment ... because he has opposed any practice made an unlawful employment practice by this subchapter, or because he has made a charge, testified, assisted, or participated in any manner in an investigation, proceeding, or hearing under this subchapter.

citations.case: Burlington Northern & Santa Fe Railway Co. v. White
citations.quote: We also conclude that the provision covers those (and only those) employer actions that would have been materially adverse to a reasonable employee or job applicant. In the present context that means that the employer’s actions must be harmful to the point that they could well dissuade a reasonable worker from making or supporting a charge of discrimination.

clauses.body: {{employeeName}} is eligible for FMLA leave only if {{employeeName}} has worked for {{companyName}} for at least 12 months, has worked at least 1,250 hours for {{companyName}} in the preceding 12-month period, and works at a location where {{companyName}} employs at least 50 employees within 75 miles.
clauses.gap: These three conditions are cumulative — missing any one of them means the employee isn't eligible under this federal law, regardless of how long they've worked there or how compelling the reason for leave is. This document doesn't determine eligibility for a specific case; it states the test.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 2611(2)(A) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Family and Medical Leave Act, eligible-employee definition
citations.quote: The term “eligible employee” means an employee who has been employed— (i) for at least 12 months by the employer with respect to whom leave is requested under section 2612 of this title; and (ii) for at least 1,250 hours of service with such employer during the previous 12-month period.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 2611(2)(B)(ii) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Family and Medical Leave Act, worksite-size exclusion
citations.quote: any employee of an employer who is employed at a worksite at which such employer employs less than 50 employees if the total number of employees employed by that employer within 75 miles of that worksite is less than 50.

clauses.title: Leave Entitlement
clauses.body: An eligible employee is entitled to 12 workweeks of leave during any 12-month period for the birth of a child and to care for the newborn; the placement of a child for adoption or foster care; to care for a spouse, child, or parent with a serious health condition; or because of the employee's own serious health condition that makes the employee unable to perform the job.
clauses.gap: This describes the four most commonly used qualifying reasons under this provision. Two more categories exist under this same law that this document doesn't cover: leave for a qualifying exigency arising from a family member's covered active military duty, and up to 26 workweeks — not 12 — in a single 12-month period to care for a covered servicemember family member.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 2612(a)(1)(A)-(D) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Family and Medical Leave Act, leave entitlement
citations.quote: an eligible employee shall be entitled to a total of 12 workweeks of leave during any 12-month period for one or more of the following: (A) Because of the birth of a son or daughter of the employee and in order to care for such son or daughter. (B) Because of the placement of a son or daughter with the employee for adoption or foster care. (C) In order to care for the spouse, or a son, daughter, or parent, of the employee, if such spouse, son, daughter, or parent has a serious health condition. (D) Because of a serious health condition that makes the employee unable to perform the functions of the position of such employee.

citations.case: 29 C.F.R. § 825.200(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Electronic Code of Federal Regulations, DOL's own restatement of the 12-workweek entitlement
citations.quote: Except in the case of leave to care for a covered servicemember with a serious injury or illness, an eligible employee's FMLA leave entitlement is limited to a total of 12 workweeks of leave during any 12-month period for any one, or more, of the following reasons: (1) The birth of the employee's son or daughter, and to care for the newborn child; (2) The placement with the employee of a son or daughter for adoption or foster care, and to care for the newly placed child; (3) To care for the employee's spouse, son, daughter, or parent with a serious health condition; (4) Because of a serious health condition that makes the employee unable to perform one or more of the essential functions

clauses.title: Military Family Leave
clauses.body: Two additional, separate categories of leave exist under the same law for military families. First, an eligible employee can take leave — still within the general 12-workweek entitlement — for a qualifying exigency arising from a spouse's, child's, or parent's covered active duty (or call to active duty) in the Armed Forces; the specific qualifying exigencies are defined by regulation, not this statute directly. Second, an eligible employee who is the spouse, child, parent, or next of kin of a covered servicemember can take up to 26 workweeks — more than double the general entitlement — in a single 12-month period to care for that servicemember, though this longer leave is available only once, not in every 12-month period.
clauses.gap: This is a real, quotable federal entitlement, not a summary — verified against the current U.S. Code text. If an employee takes both the general 12-workweek leave and the 26-week servicemember caregiver leave in the same single 12-month period, the combined total is still capped at 26 workweeks, not 38. This document doesn't state the regulatory definition of a qualifying exigency, which is set by the Department of Labor, not the statute itself.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 2612(a)(1)(E) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Family and Medical Leave Act, qualifying exigency leave
citations.quote: Because of any qualifying exigency (as the Secretary shall, by regulation, determine) arising out of the fact that the spouse, or a son, daughter, or parent of the employee is on covered active duty (or has been notified of an impending call or order to covered active duty) in the Armed Forces.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 2612(a)(3) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Family and Medical Leave Act, servicemember family leave
citations.quote: an eligible employee who is the spouse, son, daughter, parent, or next of kin of a covered servicemember shall be entitled to a total of 26 workweeks of leave during a 12-month period to care for the servicemember. The leave described in this paragraph shall only be available during a single 12-month period.

clauses.title: Returning From Leave
clauses.body: When {{employeeName}} returns from FMLA leave taken for its intended purpose, {{companyName}} must restore {{employeeName}} to the same position held before the leave, or to an equivalent position with equivalent pay, benefits, and other terms and conditions of employment. Taking FMLA leave doesn't cause {{employeeName}} to lose any employment benefit that had already accrued before the leave began.
clauses.gap: This restoration right has two real limits. First, it doesn't entitle a returning employee to accrue seniority or benefits during the leave itself, or to any right, benefit, or position better than what the employee would have had without taking leave — restoration is a floor, not an upgrade. Second, federal law lets an employer deny restoration to certain highly compensated employees — those among the highest-paid 10% within 75 miles of the facility — if restoring them would cause substantial and grievous economic injury to the business, the employer notifies the employee of that intent when it determines the injury would occur, and, if leave has already started, the employee still chooses not to return after receiving that notice.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 2614(a)(1)-(2) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Family and Medical Leave Act, restoration to position
citations.quote: any eligible employee who takes leave under section 2612 of this title for the intended purpose of the leave shall be entitled, on return from such leave— (A) to be restored by the employer to the position of employment held by the employee when the leave commenced; or (B) to be restored to an equivalent position with equivalent employment benefits, pay, and other terms and conditions of employment. ... The taking of leave under section 2612 of this title shall not result in the loss of any employment benefit accrued prior to the date on which the leave commenced.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 2614(a)(3) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Family and Medical Leave Act, limitations on restoration
citations.quote: Nothing in this section shall be construed to entitle any restored employee to— (A) the accrual of any seniority or employment benefits during any period of leave; or (B) any right, benefit, or position of employment other than any right, benefit, or position to which the employee would have been entitled had the employee not taken the leave.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 2614(b) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Family and Medical Leave Act, highly compensated employee exemption
citations.quote: An employer may deny restoration under subsection (a) to any eligible employee described in paragraph (2) if— (A) such denial is necessary to prevent substantial and grievous economic injury to the operations of the employer; (B) the employer notifies the employee of the intent of the employer to deny restoration on such basis at the time the employer determines that such injury would occur; and (C) in any case in which the leave has commenced, the employee elects not to return to employment after receiving such notice. ... An eligible employee described in paragraph (1) is a salaried eligible employee who is among the highest paid 10 percent of the employees employed by the employer within 75 miles of the facility at which the employee is employed.

clauses.title: No Interference or Retaliation
clauses.body: {{companyName}} will not interfere with, restrain, or deny {{employeeName}}'s exercise of rights under this law, and will not discharge or discriminate against {{employeeName}} for opposing a practice this law makes unlawful.
clauses.gap: This protection extends beyond someone who actually takes leave — it also covers interference with the attempt to exercise a right under this law, and separately protects anyone who has filed a charge, given information, or testified in a proceeding related to it, not just the person who requested leave.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 2615(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Family and Medical Leave Act, interference with rights
citations.quote: It shall be unlawful for any employer to interfere with, restrain, or deny the exercise of or the attempt to exercise, any right provided under this subchapter. ... It shall be unlawful for any employer to discharge or in any other manner discriminate against any individual for opposing any practice made unlawful by this subchapter.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 2615(b) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Family and Medical Leave Act, interference with proceedings or inquiries
citations.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to discharge or in any other manner discriminate against any individual because such individual— (1) has filed any charge, or has instituted or caused to be instituted any proceeding, under or related to this subchapter; (2) has given, or is about to give, any information in connection with any inquiry or proceeding relating to any right provided under this subchapter; or (3) has testified, or is about to testify, in any inquiry or proceeding relating to any right provided under this subchapter.

clauses.title: The Duty to Accommodate, and Its Limit
clauses.body: Federal law requires {{companyName}} to make reasonable accommodations for the known physical or mental limitations of a qualified employee with a disability, unless doing so would impose an undue hardship on {{companyName}}'s operations.
clauses.gap: Undue hardship isn't just about cost in isolation — the law weighs the accommodation's cost and nature against the size, financial resources, and structure of the specific employer and facility involved. The same accommodation can be reasonable for one employer and an undue hardship for a much smaller one; this document states the legal standard, not how it applies to any specific accommodation request.

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 12112(b)(5)(A) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Americans with Disabilities Act, reasonable-accommodation duty
citations.quote: not making reasonable accommodations to the known physical or mental limitations of an otherwise qualified individual with a disability who is an applicant or employee, unless such covered entity can demonstrate that the accommodation would impose an undue hardship on the operation of the business of such covered entity

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 12111(10) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Americans with Disabilities Act, undue-hardship definition and factors
citations.quote: The term “undue hardship” means an action requiring significant difficulty or expense, when considered in light of the factors set forth in subparagraph (B). ... factors to be considered include— (i) the nature and cost of the accommodation needed under this chapter; (ii) the overall financial resources of the facility or facilities involved in the provision of the reasonable accommodation; the number of persons employed at such facility; the effect on expenses and resources, or the impact otherwise of such accommodation upon the operation of the facility; (iii) the overall financial resources of the covered entity; the overall size of the business of a covered entity with respect to the number of its employees; the number, type, and location of its facilities; and (iv) the type of operation or operations of the covered entity, including the composition, structure, and functions of the workforce of such entity; the geographic separateness, administrative, or fiscal relationship of the facility or facilities in question to the covered entity.

clauses.title: Confidentiality of Medical Information
clauses.body: Medical information {{employeeName}} shares to support this request must be collected and kept on separate forms, in separate files from {{employeeName}}'s regular personnel file, and treated as confidential.
clauses.gap: This confidentiality duty has specific, narrow exceptions written into the same law: supervisors and managers may be told about necessary work restrictions and accommodations, safety personnel may be told if the condition might require emergency treatment, and government officials investigating compliance can get the relevant information on request. Confidential doesn't mean nobody involved can ever know anything about it — it means the underlying medical details stay restricted to those specific, limited circumstances, not shared freely.

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 12112(d)(4)(C) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Americans with Disabilities Act, confidentiality for current employees
citations.quote: Information obtained under subparagraph (B) regarding the medical condition or history of any employee are subject to the requirements of subparagraphs (B) and (C) of paragraph (3).

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 12112(d)(3)(B) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Americans with Disabilities Act, confidentiality requirements and exceptions
citations.quote: information obtained regarding the medical condition or history of the applicant is collected and maintained on separate forms and in separate medical files and is treated as a confidential medical record, except that— (i) supervisors and managers may be informed regarding necessary restrictions on the work or duties of the employee and necessary accommodations; (ii) first aid and safety personnel may be informed, when appropriate, if the disability might require emergency treatment; and (iii) government officials investigating compliance with this chapter shall be provided relevant information on request

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
The Default Rule
clauses.body: Federal law generally requires {{companyName}} to pay {{employeeName}} at least one and one-half times the regular rate of pay for hours worked beyond 40 in a workweek. This overtime requirement applies unless {{employeeName}}'s position qualifies for a specific exemption under federal law — classifying a position as exempt isn't a label a company can apply by choice; it depends on meeting the actual legal test below.
clauses.gap: This describes the federal floor only. Some states set a higher overtime threshold, a daily overtime requirement in addition to the weekly one, or a higher minimum salary for exemption than federal law requires — this document doesn't catalog those stricter state rules.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 207(a)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided in this section, no employer shall employ any of his employees who in any workweek is engaged in commerce or in the production of goods for commerce ... for a workweek longer than forty hours unless such employee receives compensation for his employment in excess of the hours above specified at a rate not less than one and one-half times the regular rate at which he is employed.

citations.case: 29 C.F.R. § 778.107 (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Electronic Code of Federal Regulations, DOL's own restatement of the overtime rate
citations.quote: The general overtime pay standard in section 7(a) requires that overtime must be compensated at a rate not less than one and one-half times the regular rate at which the employee is actually employed.

clauses.title: The Exemption Test
clauses.body: To qualify as exempt under the most commonly used federal exemptions — executive, administrative, and professional — a position generally must meet three conditions: the employee must be paid on a salary basis rather than by the hour; that salary must meet a minimum weekly amount set by federal regulation; and the employee's actual job duties, not their job title, must satisfy a specific duties test for the exemption being claimed. For the executive exemption specifically, that duties test requires the employee's primary duty to be managing the business or a recognized department, regularly directing the work of at least two other employees, and having real authority — or a real say — in hiring, firing, or similar personnel decisions.
clauses.gap: The administrative, professional, computer, and outside-sales exemptions each have their own separate duties test under this same set of regulations — this clause describes the executive exemption's test as one concrete example, not all five. Meeting the salary requirements alone never qualifies a position as exempt without also satisfying the duties test for whichever exemption is actually being claimed, and satisfying a duties test alone doesn't qualify a position that isn't also paid on a salary basis at or above the minimum amount.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 213(a)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Fair Labor Standards Act, white-collar exemptions
citations.quote: any employee employed in a bona fide executive, administrative, or professional capacity (including any employee employed in the capacity of academic administrative personnel or teacher in elementary or secondary schools), or in the capacity of outside salesman

citations.case: 29 C.F.R. § 541.100 (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Code of Federal Regulations, general rule for executive employees
citations.quote: The term “employee employed in a bona fide executive capacity” in section 13(a)(1) of the Act shall mean any employee: (1) Compensated on a salary basis pursuant to § 541.600 at a rate of not less than $684 per week ... exclusive of board, lodging or other facilities; (2) Whose primary duty is management of the enterprise in which the employee is employed or of a customarily recognized department or subdivision thereof; (3) Who customarily and regularly directs the work of two or more other employees; and (4) Who has the authority to hire or fire other employees or whose suggestions and recommendations as to the hiring, firing, advancement, promotion or any other change of status of other employees are given particular weight.

citations.case: 29 C.F.R. § 541.600 (Cornell LII text)

citations.quote: To qualify as an exempt executive, administrative or professional employee under section 13(a)(1) of the Act, an employee must be compensated on a salary basis at a rate of not less than $684 per week ... exclusive of board, lodging or other facilities.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Who This Covers
clauses.body: This request applies if {{companyName}} employs 15 or more people. Federal law requires accommodating a known limitation related to pregnancy, childbirth, or a related medical condition regardless of whether that limitation would separately qualify as a disability under the Americans with Disabilities Act.
clauses.gap: This is a distinct federal law from the ADA, not an extension of it — a limitation doesn't have to be severe enough to count as a disability to trigger this specific accommodation duty. This document doesn't restate the ADA's own accommodation clause; the two laws overlap in some situations but aren't the same test.

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 2000gg(2)(B)(i) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Pregnant Workers Fairness Act, covered-employer definition
citations.quote: an employer, which means a person engaged in industry affecting commerce who has 15 or more employees as defined in section 2000e(b) of this title

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 2000gg(4) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Pregnant Workers Fairness Act, known-limitation definition
citations.quote: the term “known limitation” means physical or mental condition related to, affected by, or arising out of pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions that the employee or employee’s representative has communicated to the employer whether or not such condition meets the definition of disability specified in section 3 of the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (42 U.S.C. 12102)

clauses.title: The Accommodation Duty
clauses.body: {{companyName}} must make a reasonable accommodation for {{employeeName}}'s known limitation unless doing so would impose an undue hardship. {{companyName}} can't require {{employeeName}} to accept a different accommodation than the one actually reached through the interactive process, can't require {{employeeName}} to take leave — paid or unpaid — if another reasonable accommodation would work instead, can't deny {{employeeName}} an employment opportunity because of the need to provide this accommodation, and can't take adverse action against {{employeeName}} for requesting or using one.
clauses.gap: This duty extends further than it might appear: someone temporarily unable to perform an essential job function still counts as a qualified employee entitled to this protection, if the inability is temporary, the function could be performed again in the near future, and the inability can be reasonably accommodated in the meantime. That's a real, specific carve-out this law adds — a temporary inability to do part of the job doesn't by itself remove someone from this protection.

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 2000gg-1(1)-(5) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Pregnant Workers Fairness Act, accommodation duty and prohibited practices
citations.quote: It shall be an unlawful employment practice for a covered entity to— (1) not make reasonable accommodations to the known limitations related to the pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions of a qualified employee, unless such covered entity can demonstrate that the accommodation would impose an undue hardship on the operation of the business of such covered entity; (2) require a qualified employee affected by pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions to accept an accommodation other than any reasonable accommodation arrived at through the interactive process referred to in section 2000gg(7) of this title; (3) deny employment opportunities to a qualified employee if such denial is based on the need of the covered entity to make reasonable accommodations to the known limitations related to the pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions of the qualified employee; (4) require a qualified employee to take leave, whether paid or unpaid, if another reasonable accommodation can be provided to the known limitations related to the pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions of the qualified employee; or (5) take adverse action in terms, conditions, or privileges of employment against a qualified employee on account of the employee requesting or using a reasonable accommodation to the known limitations related to the pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions of the employee.

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 2000gg(6) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Pregnant Workers Fairness Act, qualified-employee definition
citations.quote: the term “qualified employee” means an employee or applicant who, with or without reasonable accommodation, can perform the essential functions of the employment position, except that an employee or applicant shall be considered qualified if— (A) any inability to perform an essential function is for a temporary period; (B) the essential function could be performed in the near future; and (C) the inability to perform the essential function can be reasonably accommodated

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Who This Policy's Federal Protections Cover
clauses.body: This policy's protections under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act apply if {{companyName}} has a class of securities registered under the Securities Exchange Act, is required to file reports under Exchange Act section 15(d), is a subsidiary or affiliate whose financial information is included in such a company's consolidated financial statements, or is a nationally recognized statistical rating organization. They extend to that company's officers, employees, contractors, subcontractors, and agents — not just to the company directly.
clauses.gap: This is federal law written for public companies and their contractor and agent relationships, not a general private-sector whistleblower rule — a privately held company with no ties to a public company isn't covered by this specific statute. Many states have their own whistleblower-protection laws for private employers that this document doesn't state.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1514A(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Sarbanes-Oxley whistleblower protection, covered-company definition
citations.quote: No company with a class of securities registered under section 12 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1514A(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Sarbanes-Oxley whistleblower protection, extension to officers, employees, contractors, and agents
citations.quote: any officer, employee, contractor, subcontractor, or agent of such company or nationally recognized statistical rating organization, may discharge, demote, suspend, threaten, harass, or in any other manner discriminate against an employee in the terms and conditions of employment because of any lawful act done by the employee

citations.case: Lawson v. FMR LLC
citations.quote: We hold, based on the text of § 1514A, the mischief to which Congress was responding, and earlier legislation Congress drew upon, that the provision shelters employees of private contractors and subcontractors, just as it shelters employees of the public company served by the contractors and subcontractors.

clauses.title: What Counts As a Protected Report
clauses.body: Protected reports include providing information, or otherwise assisting in an investigation, about conduct an employee reasonably believes violates mail, wire, bank, or securities fraud law, an SEC rule, or federal law prohibiting fraud against shareholders — as long as the report goes to a federal regulatory or law enforcement agency, a Member or committee of Congress, or a supervisor or other person at the company with authority to investigate or address the misconduct. Filing, testifying in, or otherwise assisting a related legal proceeding is protected the same way.
clauses.gap: The standard is a reasonable, good-faith belief — a report doesn't have to turn out to be correct, or ever be proven in court, to be protected. This protects an internal report to a supervisor just as much as a report to an outside regulator; treating only external regulatory complaints as 'real' whistleblowing applies a narrower standard than the statute sets. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (18 U.S.C. § 1514A) rather than independently authored sources; no corroborating case on the reasonable-belief standard was added here.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1514A(a)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Sarbanes-Oxley whistleblower protection, protected-activity definition
citations.quote: to provide information, cause information to be provided, or otherwise assist in an investigation regarding any conduct which the employee reasonably believes constitutes a violation of section 1341, 1343, 1344, or 1348, any rule or regulation of the Securities and Exchange Commission, or any provision of Federal law relating to fraud against shareholders

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1514A(a)(1)(C) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Sarbanes-Oxley whistleblower protection, internal-supervisor reporting channel
citations.quote: a person with supervisory authority over the employee (or such other person working for the employer who has the authority to investigate, discover, or terminate misconduct)

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1514A(a)(2) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Sarbanes-Oxley whistleblower protection, participation in a related proceeding
citations.quote: to file, cause to be filed, testify, participate in, or otherwise assist in a proceeding filed or about to be filed (with any knowledge of the employer) relating to an alleged violation of section 1341, 1343, 1344, or 1348, any rule or regulation of the Securities and Exchange Commission, or any provision of Federal law relating to fraud against shareholders.

clauses.title: A Separate, Narrower Protection for SEC Reports
clauses.body: A different federal law, the Dodd-Frank Act, adds its own anti-retaliation right — with a direct right to sue in federal court and a longer filing deadline — but only for someone who meets Dodd-Frank's own definition of 'whistleblower': a person who has actually reported information to the Securities and Exchange Commission itself.
clauses.gap: This is a distinct, narrower category from the Sarbanes-Oxley protection above. The Supreme Court held that Dodd-Frank's anti-retaliation provision doesn't cover an employee who only reported a concern internally and never reported it to the SEC — that employee may still be protected under Sarbanes-Oxley, just not under Dodd-Frank's separate, SEC-reporting-specific right.

citations.case: 15 U.S.C. § 78u-6(a)(6) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Dodd-Frank Act, whistleblower definition
citations.quote: [t]he term “whistleblower” means any individual who provides, or 2 or more individuals acting jointly who provide, information relating to a violation of the securities laws to the Commission, in a manner established, by rule or regulation, by the Commission

citations.case: Digital Realty Trust, Inc. v. Somers
citations.quote: Dodd-Frank’s anti-retaliation provision does not extend to an individual, like Somers, who has not reported a violation of the securities laws to the SEC.

citations.case: 15 U.S.C. § 78u-6(h)(1)(B)(i) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Dodd-Frank Act, the direct right to sue in federal court
citations.quote: An individual who alleges discharge or other discrimination in violation of subparagraph (A) may bring an action under this subsection in the appropriate district court of the United States for the relief provided in subparagraph (C).

clauses.title: This Can't Be Signed Away
clauses.body: The rights described above can't be waived by any agreement, company policy, or condition of employment — including a predispute arbitration agreement. A predispute arbitration agreement is not valid or enforceable to the extent it would require arbitrating a dispute under this specific protection.
clauses.gap: This is a stronger, more specific rule than the general principle that a government agency's own enforcement rights survive a private arbitration agreement (see the arbitration document's coverage of that separate point) — here, the employee's own personal claim under this statute is itself exempt from a predispute arbitration requirement, not just the agency's independent authority to act. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (18 U.S.C. § 1514A) rather than independently authored sources; no corroborating case was added here.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1514A(e)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Sarbanes-Oxley whistleblower protection, non-waivability
citations.quote: The rights and remedies provided for in this section may not be waived by any agreement, policy form, or condition of employment, including by a predispute arbitration agreement.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1514A(e)(2) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Sarbanes-Oxley whistleblower protection, predispute arbitration ban
citations.quote: No predispute arbitration agreement shall be valid or enforceable, if the agreement requires arbitration of a dispute arising under this section.

clauses.title: What's Available If Retaliation Happens
clauses.body: An employee who proves retaliation under the Sarbanes-Oxley protection is entitled to reinstatement with the same seniority the employee would have had, back pay with interest, and compensation for special damages including litigation costs, expert witness fees, and reasonable attorney fees. Under the separate Dodd-Frank protection described above, back pay is doubled.
clauses.gap: The doubled back pay is specific to a Dodd-Frank claim — someone who is protected only under Sarbanes-Oxley (for example, an internal report never made to the SEC) is entitled to ordinary back pay under that statute, not the doubled amount. This document doesn't walk through how to actually bring either claim, but the two statutes set very different deadlines worth knowing exist: a Sarbanes-Oxley claim has to be started within 180 days of the violation (or of when the employee became aware of it), while a Dodd-Frank claim has up to 6 years from the violation, or 3 years from when the relevant facts were or should have been known, capped at 10 years outer limit either way.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1514A(b)(2)(D) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Sarbanes-Oxley whistleblower protection, filing deadline
citations.quote: An action under paragraph (1) shall be commenced not later than 180 days after the date on which the violation occurs, or after the date on which the employee became aware of the violation.

citations.case: 15 U.S.C. § 78u-6(h)(1)(B)(iii) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Dodd-Frank Act, filing deadline
citations.quote: (aa) more than 6 years after the date on which the violation of subparagraph (A) occurred; or (bb) more than 3 years after the date when facts material to the right of action are known or reasonably should have been known by the employee alleging a violation of subparagraph (A)

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1514A(c)(2) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Sarbanes-Oxley whistleblower protection, compensatory damages
citations.quote: reinstatement with the same seniority status that the employee would have had, but for the discrimination

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1514A(c)(2) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Sarbanes-Oxley whistleblower protection, special damages
citations.quote: compensation for any special damages sustained as a result of the discrimination, including litigation costs, expert witness fees, and reasonable attorney fees.

citations.case: 15 U.S.C. § 78u-6(h)(1)(C)(ii) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Dodd-Frank Act, doubled back pay remedy
citations.quote: 2 times the amount of back pay otherwise owed to the individual, with interest

A report may be made confidentially. Retaliation against anyone who reports in good faith is prohibited by this policy, regardless of whether the report ultimately proves a violation occurred.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Restriction
clauses.body: For {{restrictionPeriod}} after {{employeeName}}'s employment with {{companyName}} ends, {{employeeName}} will not solicit or induce, or attempt to solicit or induce, any employee of {{companyName}} to leave their employment.

clauses.title: A Genuinely Unsettled Question in Some States
clauses.body: Whether a restriction like this one — barring solicitation of a former employer's own employees, as opposed to its customers — can be enforced at all is a real, unresolved question in at least one state. California courts have gone different ways on it.
clauses.gap: In 1985, a California appellate court upheld a similar no-raiding restriction against a former executive as valid, reasoning it only slightly restrained trade. In 2018, a different panel of the same court, applying the California Supreme Court's intervening decision in Edwards v. Arthur Andersen, expressly doubted that the 1985 case remained good law, and held a similar restriction void as applied to individuals whose own profession was recruiting other people's employees. This is one state's real, citable split as evidence such uncertainty exists — not a claim about which state's law governs this specific agreement, or about how a court would rule on a different set of facts than either of these two cases.

citations.case: Loral Corp. v. Moyes
citations.quote: We hold that this contract, as construed, is not void on its face under Business and Professions Code section 16600.

citations.case: AMN Healthcare, Inc. v. Aya Healthcare Services, Inc.
citations.quote: We thus doubt the continuing viability of Moyes post-Edwards.

citations.case: AMN Healthcare, Inc. v. Aya Healthcare Services, Inc.
citations.quote: We thus independently conclude section 3.2 of the CNDA is void under section 16600.

clauses.title: This Is Different From a Customer Non-Solicitation Clause
clauses.body: A restriction on soliciting a former employer's customers is a separate question from the employee-solicitation restriction above, and in at least one state, better settled: a court there won't directly enforce a contract clause banning a former employee from soliciting former customers, though it can still stop someone from using the former employer's trade secrets to do so.
clauses.gap: This means the underlying conduct — misusing confidential information or trade secrets to go after a former employer's customers — can still be restrained through trade-secret and unfair-competition law even where the contract clause itself can't be enforced directly. The Non-Disclosure Agreement document in this set covers trade-secret obligations separately; this document doesn't restate them.

citations.case: AMN Healthcare, Inc. v. Aya Healthcare Services, Inc.
citations.cite: 28 Cal. App. 5th 923 (2018), quoting The Retirement Group v. Galante, 176 Cal. App. 4th 1226 (2009)
citations.quote: specifically enforcing . . . a contractual clause purporting to ban a former employee from soliciting former customers to transfer their business away from the former employer to the employee's new business, but a court may enjoin tortious conduct ... by banning the former employee from using trade secret information to identify existing customers, to facilitate the solicitation of such customers, or to otherwise unfairly compete with the former employer.

citations.case: Muggill v. Reuben H. Donnelley Corp.
citations.cite: 62 Cal. 2d 239, 242 (1965), quoted in Loral Corp. v. Moyes, 174 Cal. App. 3d 268, 275-76 (1985)
citations.quote: unless they are necessary to protect the employer's trade secrets

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Formation and Membership
clauses.body: {{companyName}} is a single-member limited liability company organized under the laws of {{stateOfFormation}}. {{memberName}} is its sole member, holding a 100% membership interest.

clauses.title: Federal Tax Classification
clauses.body: For federal tax purposes, {{companyName}} is, by default, disregarded as an entity separate from {{memberName}} — its income, deductions, and credits are reported on {{memberName}}'s own tax return, rather than a separate company return, unless {{companyName}} affirmatively elects a different classification.
clauses.gap: This default applies automatically, with no election required — but it isn't the only option. A single-member LLC can elect to be taxed as a corporation, or potentially as an S corporation through a separate election, by filing the appropriate IRS form. This document doesn't say which classification is actually better for a given business — that depends on income level, self-employment tax exposure, and other facts specific to the business. Being disregarded for federal tax purposes has no effect on the LLC's separate legal existence under state law; those are two different questions, addressed by two different bodies of law. This is one federal regulation; no additional independent source was found restating this specific default classification separately.

citations.case: 26 C.F.R. § 301.7701-3(b)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Treasury Regulations, default federal tax classification of eligible entities (the 'check-the-box' rule)
citations.quote: unless the entity elects otherwise, a domestic eligible entity is— (i) A partnership if it has two or more members; or (ii) Disregarded as an entity separate from its owner if it has a single owner.

clauses.title: How and When a Different Classification Gets Elected
clauses.body: Changing away from the default disregarded-entity treatment isn't automatic — it takes filing IRS Form 8832 (Entity Classification Election). The effective date on that form has real limits: it can't be dated more than 75 days before the filing date, and can't be dated more than 12 months after it. Once {{companyName}} makes an election to change its classification, it generally can't elect a different classification again for 60 months from the effective date of that election, absent IRS permission.
clauses.gap: This is one federal rule, verified against the current Treasury Regulations text. The 60-month lock-in has a narrow exception — the IRS may allow an earlier change if more than half the entity's ownership as of the later election is held by people who owned no interest at the time of the earlier one — but that relief isn't automatic, and this document doesn't state the full standard for obtaining it. This document doesn't cover the separate, S-corporation-specific election under 26 U.S.C. § 1362, which has its own timing rule.

citations.case: 26 C.F.R. § 301.7701-3(c)(1)(i) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Treasury Regulations, how an eligible entity elects its classification
citations.quote: an eligible entity may elect to be classified other than as provided under paragraph (b) of this section, or to change its classification, by filing Form 8832, Entity Classification Election, with the service center designated on Form 8832.

citations.case: 26 C.F.R. § 301.7701-3(c)(1)(iii) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Treasury Regulations, the effective-date window for a classification election
citations.quote: The effective date specified on Form 8832 can not be more than 75 days prior to the date on which the election is filed and can not be more than 12 months after the date on which the election is filed.

citations.case: 26 C.F.R. § 301.7701-3(c)(1)(iv) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Treasury Regulations, the sixty-month limitation on re-electing
citations.quote: If an eligible entity makes an election under paragraph (c)(1)(i) of this section to change its classification (other than an election made by an existing entity to change its classification as of the effective date of this section), the entity cannot change its classification by election again during the sixty months succeeding the effective date of the election.

clauses.title: Limited Liability
clauses.body: {{companyName}}'s debts and liabilities are its own — they don't become {{memberName}}'s personal debts or liabilities solely because {{memberName}} is its member.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used here as real evidence that a liability shield with a specific, real exception is a genuine feature of LLC law generally — not a claim about which state's law actually governs this company. The shield isn't absolute: a member can still be held personally liable under the common-law 'alter ego' doctrine, the same doctrine that can pierce a corporation's liability shield, under the same or similar circumstances. One thing that specifically does not count against a member on its own, at least under this statute: failing to hold formal member or manager meetings doesn't establish alter ego liability by itself, as long as the articles of organization or the operating agreement itself doesn't require holding them.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17703.04(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, liability shield
citations.quote: All of the following apply to debts, obligations, or other liabilities of a limited liability company, whether arising in contract, tort, or otherwise: (1) They are solely the debts, obligations, or other liabilities of the limited liability company to which the debts, obligations, or other liabilities relate. (2) They do not become the debts, obligations, or other liabilities of a member or manager solely by reason of the member acting as a member or manager acting as a manager for the limited liability company.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17703.04(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, alter ego liability and the meeting-formalities carve-out
citations.quote: A member of a limited liability company shall be subject to liability under the common law governing alter ego liability, and shall also be personally liable under a judgment of a court or for any debt, obligation, or liability of the limited liability company, whether that liability or obligation arises in contract, tort, or otherwise, under the same or similar circumstances and to the same extent as a shareholder of a corporation may be personally liable for any debt, obligation, or liability of the corporation; except that the failure to hold meetings of members or managers or the failure to observe formalities pertaining to the calling or conduct of meetings shall not be considered a factor tending to establish that a member or the members have alter ego or personal liability for any debt, obligation, or liability of the limited liability company where the articles of organization or operating agreement do not expressly require the holding of meetings of members or managers.

clauses.title: Records and Tax Return Access
clauses.body: A member — or someone a member's interest in {{companyName}} has been transferred to — has the right, for purposes reasonably related to their interest, to inspect and copy {{companyName}}'s required records during normal business hours, and to obtain a written copy of {{companyName}}'s federal, state, and local income tax returns for each year, promptly after they become available.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine default access right — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC. This right belongs to a transferee (someone who receives an economic interest, such as an heir, without becoming a full member) as well as to members themselves — it isn't limited to people with voting rights. This document doesn't restate the additional annual and interim financial-reporting duties this same statute imposes once an LLC has more than 35 members.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.10(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, member and transferee inspection and tax-return rights
citations.quote: Each member, manager, and transferee has the right, upon reasonable request, for purposes reasonably related to the interest of that person as a member, manager, or transferee, to each of the following: (1) To inspect and copy during normal business hours any of the records required to be maintained pursuant to Section 17701.13. (2) To obtain in writing from the limited liability company, promptly after becoming available, a copy of the limited liability company’s federal, state, and local income tax returns for each year.

clauses.body: {{companyName}} will continue until dissolved by {{memberName}} or as otherwise required by law. Upon dissolution, {{companyName}}'s debts and liabilities will be paid or provided for first, with any remaining assets distributed to {{memberName}}.

clauses.title: What Happens on the Sole Member's Death
clauses.body: A single-member LLC does not automatically dissolve the moment its sole member dies. State law's default dissolution trigger for a membership gap is 90 consecutive days with no members — but on the death of a sole member, that member's interest can pass directly to their heirs, successors, or assigns by will or other applicable law, and that heir or successor becomes a substituted member without needing anyone's permission or consent.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine default succession rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC. This default rule doesn't override estate administration itself — the interest still passes subject to whatever probate or other administration process otherwise applies to the deceased member's estate. This document doesn't say who the heir, successor, or assign actually is for a given member; that's a matter of the member's own estate plan (or intestacy law if there isn't one), not something this operating agreement can settle on its own.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.01(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, sole member's death and heir succession
citations.quote: The passage of 90 consecutive days during which the limited liability company has no members, except that, on the death of a natural person who is the sole member of a limited liability company, the status of the member, including a membership interest, may pass to one or more heirs, successors, and assigns of the member by will or applicable law. An heir, successor, or assign of the member’s interest becomes a substituted member pursuant to paragraph (4) of subdivision (c) of Section 17704.01, subject to administration as provided by applicable law, without the permission or consent of the heirs, successors, or assigns or those administering the estate of the deceased member.

clauses.title: Federal Tax Classification
clauses.body: For federal tax purposes, {{companyName}} is, by default, classified as a partnership — its income, deductions, and credits pass through to its members' own tax returns, rather than {{companyName}} paying tax at the entity level, unless {{companyName}} affirmatively elects a different classification.
clauses.gap: This default applies automatically, with no election required — but it isn't the only option. A multi-member LLC can elect to be taxed as a corporation, or potentially as an S corporation through a separate election, by filing the appropriate IRS form. This document doesn't say which classification is actually better for a given business — that depends on income level, self-employment tax exposure, and other facts specific to the business. Partnership tax treatment brings its own requirements this document doesn't cover, including that the LLC generally must file its own annual information return (Form 1065) even though it doesn't pay entity-level tax itself. This is one federal regulation; no additional independent source was found restating this specific default classification separately.

citations.case: 26 C.F.R. § 301.7701-3(b)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Treasury Regulations, default federal tax classification of eligible entities (the 'check-the-box' rule)
citations.quote: unless the entity elects otherwise, a domestic eligible entity is— (i) A partnership if it has two or more members; or (ii) Disregarded as an entity separate from its owner if it has a single owner.

clauses.title: Limited Liability
clauses.body: {{companyName}}'s debts and liabilities are its own — they don't become a member's personal debts or liabilities solely because that person is a member.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used here as real evidence that a liability shield with a specific, real exception is a genuine feature of LLC law generally — not a claim about which state's law actually governs this company. The shield isn't absolute: a member can still be held personally liable under the common-law 'alter ego' doctrine, the same doctrine that can pierce a corporation's liability shield, under the same or similar circumstances. One thing that specifically does not count against a member on its own, at least under this statute: failing to hold formal member or manager meetings doesn't establish alter ego liability by itself, as long as the articles of organization or the operating agreement itself doesn't require holding them.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17703.04(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, liability shield
citations.quote: All of the following apply to debts, obligations, or other liabilities of a limited liability company, whether arising in contract, tort, or otherwise: (1) They are solely the debts, obligations, or other liabilities of the limited liability company to which the debts, obligations, or other liabilities relate. (2) They do not become the debts, obligations, or other liabilities of a member or manager solely by reason of the member acting as a member or manager acting as a manager for the limited liability company.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17703.04(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, alter ego liability and the meeting-formalities carve-out
citations.quote: A member of a limited liability company shall be subject to liability under the common law governing alter ego liability, and shall also be personally liable under a judgment of a court or for any debt, obligation, or liability of the limited liability company, whether that liability or obligation arises in contract, tort, or otherwise, under the same or similar circumstances and to the same extent as a shareholder of a corporation may be personally liable for any debt, obligation, or liability of the corporation; except that the failure to hold meetings of members or managers or the failure to observe formalities pertaining to the calling or conduct of meetings shall not be considered a factor tending to establish that a member or the members have alter ego or personal liability for any debt, obligation, or liability of the limited liability company where the articles of organization or operating agreement do not expressly require the holding of meetings of members or managers.

clauses.body:

clauses.title: Fiduciary Duties — and Who Actually Owes Them
clauses.body: Which management box is checked above changes who owes what to whom. If {{companyName}} is member-managed, each member owes the company and the other members a duty of loyalty — to account for and hold as trustee any property, profit, or benefit the member takes from the company or a company opportunity; to avoid dealing with the company on behalf of someone whose interests are adverse to it; and to avoid competing with the company — plus a duty of care limited to avoiding grossly negligent or reckless conduct, intentional misconduct, or a knowing violation of law (ordinary negligence isn't enough to breach it). If {{companyName}} is manager-managed instead, those same duties shift to the manager or managers — a member who isn't also a manager owes no fiduciary duty to the company or the other members solely because they're a member.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine default duty structure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC. A member doesn't breach these duties merely by acting in their own self-interest — the statute says so directly. Everyone still owes the company and the other members an obligation of good faith and fair dealing, regardless of which management structure applies; that obligation isn't one of the two duties that shifts to managers only.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.09(b)-(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, a member's duties of loyalty and care
citations.quote: A member’s duty of loyalty to the limited liability company and the other members is limited to the following: (1) To account to the limited liability company and hold as trustee for it any property, profit, or benefit derived by the member in the conduct and winding up of the activities of a limited liability company or derived from a use by the member of a limited liability company property, including the appropriation of a limited liability company opportunity. (2) To refrain from dealing with the limited liability company in the conduct or winding up of the activities of the limited liability company as or on behalf of a person having an interest adverse to the limited liability company. (3) To refrain from competing with the limited liability company in the conduct or winding up of the activities of the limited liability company.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.09(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, duties shift to the manager in a manager-managed LLC
citations.quote: In a manager-managed limited liability company, all of the following rules apply: (1) Subdivisions (a), (b), (c), and (e) apply to the manager or managers and not the members. (2) Subdivision (d) applies to the members and managers. (3) Except as otherwise provided, a member does not have any fiduciary duty to the limited liability company or to any other member solely by reason of being a member.

clauses.title: Distributions
clauses.body: Distributions of available cash or property are made among the members as set forth in this agreement. Members may set any distribution arrangement they choose in this document — it doesn't have to match ownership percentages.
clauses.gap: This is one state's default rule, useful as real evidence of what happens if an operating agreement doesn't actually state how distributions are shared: rather than splitting by ownership percentage, the default is based on the value of each member's contributions. That default can produce a genuinely surprising result — a member with a stated ownership percentage that doesn't match their actual capital contribution (a common setup for a member contributing services rather than cash) could receive far less than their ownership percentage would suggest, or nothing at all, unless the agreement itself sets a different rule. Separately, under this same default framework, a member who leaves the company isn't automatically entitled to a distribution just because they left, unless the company's governing documents say otherwise. This is exactly why this document states the members' agreed-upon arrangement directly, rather than leaving it to whatever the state default happens to be. This is one state's default rule, cited as real evidence — not a claim about which state's law actually governs this company.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.04(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, default distribution rule
citations.quote: Any distributions made by a limited liability company before its dissolution and winding up shall be among the members in accordance with the operating agreement. If the operating agreement does not otherwise provide, distributions shall be on the basis of the value, as stated in the required records when the limited liability company decides to make the distribution, of the contributions the limited liability company has received from each member

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.04(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, dissociation doesn't itself trigger a distribution
citations.quote: Unless the articles of organization or written operating agreement provides otherwise, a person’s dissociation does not entitle the person to a distribution

clauses.title: The Default Dissolution Triggers
clauses.body: Absent a different rule in the operating agreement or articles of organization, state law dissolves an LLC on the first of several events: an event the operating agreement or articles specifically designate; a vote of members holding 50% or more of the voting interests (or a higher percentage, if the operating agreement sets one); 90 consecutive days with no members at all; or a court's decree of judicial dissolution.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual default trigger set — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC. The statutory member-vote default is 50% or more, not a majority exceeding 50% — a small but real difference from a "more than half" threshold, worth checking against whatever specific vote requirement this agreement's own management section actually sets. This document doesn't cover the separate grounds for judicial dissolution itself, which is a distinct statutory process from the events listed here.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.01 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, default dissolution triggers
citations.quote: A limited liability company is dissolved, and its activities shall be wound up, upon the happening of the first to occur of the following: (a) On the happening of an event set forth in a written operating agreement or the articles of organization. (b) By the vote of 50 percent or more of the voting interests of the members of the limited liability company or a greater percentage of the voting interests of members as may be specified in the articles of organization, or a written operating agreement.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.01(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, the no-members trigger
