clauses.title: Purpose
clauses.body: These are the bylaws of {{companyName}}, a corporation organized under the laws of {{stateOfFormation}}. They govern the internal affairs of the corporation until amended as provided below.

clauses.title: Shareholder Meetings
clauses.body: Unless the articles of incorporation say otherwise, a quorum for a shareholders' meeting is a majority of the shares entitled to vote, present in person or by proxy — though it can never be less than one-third of the shares entitled to vote (20% instead, for a mutual water company), and (except for a close corporation) never more than a majority either. Once a quorum is present, a matter passes with the affirmative vote of a majority of the shares actually represented and voting at the meeting, unless a bigger vote is required by law or the articles.
clauses.gap: This is one state's default rule, used here as real evidence of what a corporation gets automatically if its own bylaws don't set a different quorum or voting threshold — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. The quorum requirement is boxed in on both sides by statute in this state: bylaws can't set it below one-third (or 20% for a mutual water company), and — unless the corporation is a close corporation — can't set it above a majority either. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 602) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 602(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, shareholder meeting quorum floor and ceiling
citations.quote: Unless otherwise provided in the articles, a majority of the shares entitled to vote, represented in person or by proxy, shall constitute a quorum at a meeting of the shareholders, but in no event shall a quorum consist of less than one-third (or, in the case of a mutual water company, 20 percent) of the shares entitled to vote at the meeting or, except in the case of a close corporation, of more than a majority of the shares entitled to vote at the meeting.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 602(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, shareholder voting threshold
citations.quote: Except as provided in subdivision (b), the affirmative vote of a majority of the shares represented and voting at a duly held meeting at which a quorum is present (which shares voting affirmatively also constitute at least a majority of the required quorum) shall be the act of the shareholders, unless the vote of a greater number or voting by classes is required by this division or the articles.

clauses.title: If Shareholders Leave Mid-Meeting
clauses.body: Once a quorum is present at a properly called shareholders' meeting, the meeting doesn't automatically lose its authority to act just because enough shareholders leave to drop attendance below quorum. The shareholders who remain may keep transacting business, as long as whatever they approve (other than an adjournment) gets the affirmative vote of at least a majority of the shares it would have taken to make a quorum in the first place — or a bigger vote, if a bigger vote was otherwise required for that action.
clauses.gap: This is one state's default rule, used here as real evidence of a genuine feature of shareholder-meeting procedure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. This means a shareholder can't block action simply by walking out once a quorum has already been established; the practical check is the majority-of-quorum vote threshold, not attendance at the moment of the vote. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 602(b)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 602(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, meeting continues despite a walkout
citations.quote: The shareholders present at a duly called or held meeting at which a quorum is present may continue to transact business until adjournment notwithstanding the withdrawal of enough shareholders to leave less than a quorum, if any action taken (other than adjournment) is approved by at least a majority of the shares required to constitute a quorum

clauses.title: Acting Without a Meeting
clauses.body: Shareholders can generally approve most actions in writing, without holding a meeting at all, as long as shareholders holding at least the number of votes it would take to approve that action at a meeting sign a written consent. Electing directors is a real exception to that rule: directors can't be elected by written consent unless every single share entitled to vote signs on — a bare or even large majority isn't enough — with one narrow carve-out: shareholders can fill a board vacancy (other than one created by removing a director) by written consent of a majority of the outstanding voting shares.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine formal requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. A shareholder who signs a consent can revoke it, but only before the required number of consents needed to approve the action have actually been filed with the corporation — not after. Separately, unless every voting shareholder consented in writing, the statute requires notice to shareholders who didn't sign, timed differently depending on what kind of action was approved. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 603) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 603(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, general written-consent mechanism
citations.quote: Unless otherwise provided in the articles, any action that may be taken at any annual or special meeting of shareholders may be taken without a meeting and without prior notice, if a consent in writing, as specified in Section 195, setting forth the action so taken, shall be provided by the holders of outstanding shares having not less than the minimum number of votes that would be necessary to authorize or take that action at a meeting at which all shares entitled to vote thereon were present and voted.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 603(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, directors generally can't be elected by less than unanimous consent
citations.quote: Notwithstanding subdivision (a), directors may not be elected by written consent except by unanimous written consent of all shares entitled to vote for the election of directors; provided that the shareholders may elect a director to fill a vacancy, other than a vacancy created by removal, by the written consent of a majority of the outstanding shares entitled to vote.

clauses.title: Board of Directors
clauses.body: The number of directors shall be _______. Directors are elected by the shareholders at each annual meeting and serve until the next annual meeting or until a successor is elected.

clauses.title: Cumulative Voting for Directors
clauses.body: Shareholders have a default right to cumulative voting in director elections, subject to certain exceptions (classified boards and short-slate voting under other sections, discussed below): instead of casting one vote per share for each open board seat, a shareholder can give one candidate a number of votes equal to the number of directors being elected multiplied by that shareholder's normal vote count, or spread those same total votes across several candidates as they choose. That right doesn't activate automatically at a given meeting — it requires that a candidate's name was placed in nomination before the voting, and that some shareholder gave notice at the meeting, before voting began, of an intention to cumulate votes. Once any one shareholder gives that notice, every shareholder at that meeting may cumulate their votes.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine default shareholder right — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. Cumulative voting is a real protection for minority shareholders — it lets a large-enough minority concentrate their votes to elect at least one director, something they generally couldn't do if every seat were decided on a simple one-vote-per-share, highest-vote-getters basis. This right doesn't apply the same way to every corporation: it's subject to two statutory exceptions this document doesn't detail (classified-board and short-slate-voting rules under other sections), and it doesn't apply at all to a mutual water company's shareholders unless that company's own articles or bylaws say it does. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 708) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 708(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the cumulative voting mechanism
citations.quote: Except as provided in Sections 301.5 and 708.5, every shareholder complying with subdivision (b) and entitled to vote at any election of directors may cumulate such shareholder’s votes and give one candidate a number of votes equal to the number of directors to be elected multiplied by the number of votes to which the shareholder’s shares are normally entitled, or distribute the shareholder’s votes on the same principle among as many candidates as the shareholder thinks fit.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 708(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the notice precondition for cumulative voting
citations.quote: No shareholder shall be entitled to cumulate votes (i.e., cast for any candidate a number of votes greater than the number of votes that the shareholder normally is entitled to cast) unless the candidate or candidates’ names have been placed in nomination prior to the voting and the shareholder has given notice at the meeting prior to the voting of the shareholder’s intention to cumulate the shareholder’s votes. If any one shareholder has given that notice, all shareholders may cumulate their votes for candidates in nomination.

clauses.title: Removing a Director Before Their Term Ends
clauses.body: Shareholders can generally remove one or more directors without cause, by the same kind of vote it would take to elect them. But that power has a real limit tied directly to cumulative voting: a director can't be removed (unless the whole board is removed at once) if the votes cast against removal would have been enough to elect that director in the first place, assuming they'd been cast cumulatively in an election for the board's full authorized size. A corporation with a classified board is a real exception to that limit — it gets a separate, differently worded cumulative-voting test instead.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine minority-shareholder protection — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. This protection exists specifically because of cumulative voting: it prevents a bare majority from simply voting out a director whom a large-enough minority elected using their cumulative-voting power, which would otherwise make that minority protection meaningless. Reducing the authorized number of directors, or amending the bylaws to reduce board classes, doesn't itself remove a sitting director before their term is up. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 303) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 303(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, removal without cause and the cumulative-voting protection
citations.quote: Any or all of the directors may be removed without cause if the removal is approved by the outstanding shares (Section 152), subject to the following: (1) Except for a corporation to which paragraph (3) is applicable, no director may be removed (unless the entire board is removed) when the votes cast against removal, or not consenting in writing to the removal, would be sufficient to elect the director if voted cumulatively at an election at which the same total number of votes were cast (or, if the action is taken by written consent, all shares entitled to vote were voted) and the entire number of directors authorized at the time of the director’s most recent election were then being elected.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 303(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the separate test for a classified board
citations.quote: A director of a corporation whose board of directors is classified pursuant to Section 301.5 may not be removed if the votes cast against removal of the director, or not consenting in writing to the removal, would be sufficient to elect the director if voted cumulatively (without regard to whether shares may otherwise be voted cumulatively) at an election at which the same total number of votes were cast (or, if the action is taken by written consent, all shares entitled to vote were voted) and either the number of directors elected at the most recent annual meeting of shareholders, or if greater, the number of directors for whom removal is being sought, were then being elected.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 303(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, reducing the board doesn't remove a sitting director
citations.quote: Any reduction of the authorized number of directors or amendment reducing the number of classes of directors does not remove any director prior to the expiration of the director’s term of office.

clauses.title: Board Meetings
clauses.body: Unless the bylaws provide otherwise, a majority of the authorized number of directors constitutes a quorum for a board meeting, and a decision made by a majority of the directors present at a meeting where a quorum exists is the act of the board — except for certain interested-director transactions and indemnification decisions covered elsewhere in this same corporate law, which carry their own, different approval requirements a plain majority doesn't automatically satisfy.
clauses.gap: This state's statute puts a real floor under how low a corporation can set board quorum by bylaw: never less than one-third of the authorized number of directors, and never less than two — unless the corporation has only one director, in which case that one director is a quorum. The statute also bars the bylaws from letting fewer than a majority of directors present decide a matter; a corporation can require a bigger majority for board decisions, but can't require a smaller one. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence these floors are a genuine feature of corporate law generally, not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 307) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 307(a)(7) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, board meeting quorum
citations.quote: A majority of the authorized number of directors constitutes a quorum of the board for the transaction of business. The articles or bylaws may not provide that a quorum shall be less than one-third the authorized number of directors or less than two, whichever is larger, unless the authorized number of directors is one, in which case one director constitutes a quorum.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 307(a)(8) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, act of the board
citations.quote: An act or decision done or made by a majority of the directors present at a meeting duly held at which a quorum is present is the act of the board, subject to the provisions of Section 310 and subdivision (e) of Section 317.

clauses.title: Calling and Noticing Board Meetings
clauses.body: A regular board meeting can be held without any notice at all, as long as the bylaws or the board have already fixed its time and place. A special meeting is different: it requires at least four days' notice by mail, or 48 hours' notice delivered personally, by telephone (including voicemail), or electronically. Unlike quorum, this is a floor the bylaws can't lower — they cannot do away with notice of a special meeting altogether. Directors don't have to meet in person: participating by conference telephone or video counts as being present, as long as everyone can hear each other.
clauses.gap: This is one state's default rule, used here as real evidence of a genuine formal requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. A director who shows up to a meeting without objecting to a lack of notice, or who signs a written waiver, can't later challenge that meeting for lack of notice — but that's a separate, narrower point from whether notice was required in the first place. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 307) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 307(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, notice for regular vs. special board meetings
citations.quote: Regular meetings of the board may be held without notice if the time and place of the meetings are fixed by the bylaws or the board. Special meetings of the board shall be held upon four days’ notice by mail or 48 hours’ notice delivered personally or by telephone, including a voice messaging system or by electronic transmission by the corporation (Section 20). The articles or bylaws may not dispense with notice of a special meeting.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 307(a)(6) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, remote participation counts as presence
citations.quote: Participation in a meeting through use of conference telephone or electronic video screen communication pursuant to this subdivision constitutes presence in person at that meeting as long as all members participating in the meeting are able to hear one another

clauses.title: Officers
clauses.body: The officers of {{companyName}} are a president, a secretary, and a treasurer, each appointed by the board of directors and serving at the board's discretion. The same person may hold more than one office. The board may also appoint one or more vice presidents or other officers as it determines necessary.

clauses.title: Indemnification
clauses.body: {{companyName}} may indemnify a director, officer, employee, or other agent who is or was a party to a legal proceeding because of that role, against expenses, judgments, fines, and settlements actually and reasonably incurred, if that person acted in good faith and in a manner reasonably believed to be in the corporation's best interests — and, in a criminal proceeding, had no reasonable cause to believe the conduct was unlawful.
clauses.gap: This power is permissive under this statute — it authorizes indemnification but doesn't by itself require it; a corporation that wants indemnification to be guaranteed, not discretionary, typically has to say so explicitly in its own bylaws or a separate agreement. A real, important limitation: this specific rule is narrower for a proceeding brought by or in the right of the corporation itself (a derivative suit) — indemnification for amounts a person is found liable to the corporation for is barred in that kind of case unless a court specifically determines the person is fairly and reasonably entitled to it, even where the general good-faith standard above would otherwise be met. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what indemnification powers and limits typically look like — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 317) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 317(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, permissive power to indemnify
citations.quote: A corporation shall have power to indemnify any person who was or is a party or is threatened to be made a party to any proceeding (other than an action by or in the right of the corporation to procure a judgment in its favor) by reason of the fact that the person is or was an agent of the corporation, against expenses, judgments, fines, settlements, and other amounts actually and reasonably incurred in connection with the proceeding if that person acted in good faith and in a manner the person reasonably believed to be in the best interests of the corporation and, in the case of a criminal proceeding, had no reasonable cause to believe the conduct of the person was unlawful.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 317(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, derivative-suit limitation on indemnification
citations.quote: No indemnification shall be made under this subdivision for any of the following: (1) In respect of any claim, issue or matter as to which the person shall have been adjudged to be liable to the corporation in the performance of that person’s duty to the corporation and its shareholders, unless and only to the extent that the court in which the proceeding is or was pending shall determine upon application that, in view of all the circumstances of the case, the person is fairly and reasonably entitled to indemnity for expenses and then only to the extent that the court shall determine.

clauses.title: When Indemnification Isn't Optional
clauses.body: Everything above is a power {{companyName}} may exercise, not a promise — except in one specific situation, where indemnification stops being discretionary: if a director, officer, employee, or other agent is successful on the merits in defending a proceeding (or a specific claim or issue within it), the corporation must indemnify that person for the expenses actually and reasonably incurred defending it.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine mandatory floor underneath the general discretionary indemnification power — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. "Successful on the merits" is a narrower outcome than simply avoiding liability (for example, a case settled or dismissed on procedural grounds may not qualify), so this mandatory right shouldn't be assumed to cover every favorable outcome. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 317(d)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 317(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, mandatory indemnification for success on the merits
citations.quote: To the extent that an agent of a corporation has been successful on the merits in defense of any proceeding referred to in subdivision (b) or (c) or in defense of any claim, issue, or matter therein, the agent shall be indemnified against expenses actually and reasonably incurred by the agent in connection therewith.

clauses.title: Advancing Defense Costs
clauses.body: {{companyName}} may pay a director, officer, employee, or other agent's litigation expenses as they're incurred, before the proceeding is even over, rather than waiting to reimburse them only after a final determination that indemnification is proper. That advance comes with a condition: the person receiving it must first agree, in writing, to repay the money if it turns out later that they weren't actually entitled to be indemnified.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine mechanism — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. Like the general indemnification power itself, advancement here is something the corporation may do, not something it automatically must do, unless the corporation's own bylaws or a separate agreement commits to it. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 317(f)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 317(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, advancement of defense expenses
citations.quote: Expenses incurred in defending any proceeding may be advanced by the corporation prior to the final disposition of the proceeding upon receipt of an undertaking by or on behalf of the agent to repay that amount if it shall be determined ultimately that the agent is not entitled to be indemnified as authorized in this section.

clauses.title: Amendment
clauses.body: These bylaws may be amended by the affirmative vote of a majority of the directors then in office, or by the affirmative vote of a majority of the shares entitled to vote, unless the articles of incorporation or applicable law require a greater vote for a specific amendment.

clauses.title: Eligibility
clauses.body: {{companyName}} can qualify to elect S corporation tax treatment only if it meets the federal 'small business corporation' test: a domestic corporation that isn't a bank, insurance company, or certain other ineligible corporation, and that doesn't have more than 100 shareholders, doesn't have a shareholder that isn't an individual (other than certain estates and trusts), doesn't have a nonresident alien as a shareholder, and doesn't have more than one class of stock.
clauses.gap: The 100-shareholder count isn't a strict headcount of every person who owns stock — federal law treats all members of a single family, and their estates, as one shareholder for this purpose, which can make the practical limit much higher than 100 individual people. This document doesn't state which businesses would actually benefit from S corporation treatment — that depends on income level, how owners are paid, and other facts specific to the business. This is one federal rule; no additional independent source was found restating this specific eligibility test separately.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 1361(b)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, small business corporation eligibility test
citations.quote: the term “small business corporation” means a domestic corporation which is not an ineligible corporation and which does not— (A) have more than 100 shareholders, (B) have as a shareholder a person (other than an estate, a trust described in subsection (c)(2), or an organization described in subsection (c)(6)) who is not an individual, (C) have a nonresident alien as a shareholder, and (D) have more than 1 class of stock.

clauses.title: Counting Shareholders: the Family Rule
clauses.body: The 100-shareholder cap doesn't count every stockholder individually: a husband and wife (and their estates) count as one shareholder, and so does an entire family — a common ancestor plus that ancestor's lineal descendants and their spouses or former spouses — no matter how many of them actually hold stock. There's a limit to how far back the family line can be traced for this purpose: an individual doesn't count as the common ancestor if, as of the relevant date, they're more than six generations removed from the youngest generation of shareholders who would otherwise be treated as part of the family.
clauses.gap: This is one federal rule, verified against the current U.S. Code text. It only addresses how shareholders are counted toward the 100-shareholder cap — it doesn't change who is eligible to be a shareholder at all (the separate rules on individuals, estates, trusts, and nonresident aliens still apply).

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 1361(c)(1)(A)-(B) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, members of a family treated as one shareholder
citations.quote: For purposes of subsection (b)(1)(A), there shall be treated as one shareholder— (i) a husband and wife (and their estates), and (ii) all members of a family (and their estates).

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 1361(c)(1)(B)(i) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, who counts as a member of the family
citations.quote: The term “members of a family” means a common ancestor, any lineal descendant of such common ancestor, and any spouse or former spouse of such common ancestor or any such lineal descendant.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 1361(c)(1)(B)(ii) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, the six-generation limit
citations.quote: An individual shall not be considered to be a common ancestor if, on the applicable date, the individual is more than 6 generations removed from the youngest generation of shareholders who would (but for this subparagraph) be members of the family.

clauses.title: What Doesn't Count as a Second Class of Stock
clauses.body: Two structures common in small corporations don't by themselves violate the one-class-of-stock eligibility rule: giving some shares more voting power than others while keeping the same economic rights (for example, voting and non-voting common stock), and straight debt — a written, unconditional promise to pay a fixed sum on demand or on a set date, where the interest rate and payment dates aren't tied to profits, the borrower's discretion, or similar factors, that isn't convertible into stock, and that's held by someone eligible to be an S corporation shareholder (or a bank or similar lender in the ordinary course of lending).
clauses.gap: This is one federal rule, verified against the current U.S. Code text.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 1361(c)(4) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, voting-rights differences among common stock disregarded
citations.quote: For purposes of subsection (b)(1)(D), a corporation shall not be treated as having more than 1 class of stock solely because there are differences in voting rights among the shares of common stock.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 1361(c)(5)(A) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, straight debt safe harbor
citations.quote: For purposes of subsection (b)(1)(D), straight debt shall not be treated as a second class of stock.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 1361(c)(5)(B) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, the full definition of straight debt
citations.quote: For purposes of this paragraph, the term “straight debt” means any written unconditional promise to pay on demand or on a specified date a sum certain in money if— (i) the interest rate (and interest payment dates) are not contingent on profits, the borrower’s discretion, or similar factors, (ii) there is no convertibility (directly or indirectly) into stock, and (iii) the creditor is an individual (other than a nonresident alien), an estate, a trust described in paragraph (2), or a person which is actively and regularly engaged in the business of lending money.

clauses.title: Shareholder Consent
clauses.body: An S corporation election is only valid if every person who is a shareholder on the day the election is made consents to it.
clauses.gap: This is a real, all-or-nothing requirement — a single non-consenting shareholder can block the election entirely, no matter how small that shareholder's stake is. This is one federal rule; no additional independent source was found restating this specific consent requirement separately.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 1362(a)(2) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, unanimous shareholder consent requirement
citations.quote: An election under this subsection shall be valid only if all persons who are shareholders in such corporation on the day on which such election is made consent to such election.

clauses.title: When the Election Must Be Made
clauses.body: {{companyName}} can make an S corporation election either at any time during the tax year before the one it's meant to take effect for, or during that tax year itself, as long as it's made by the 15th day of the third month of that tax year.
clauses.gap: Missing this deadline doesn't necessarily end the option — the IRS has authority to accept a late election where there was reasonable cause for the delay, though that relief isn't automatic and this document doesn't state what qualifies as reasonable cause. Absent such relief, an election made after the deadline is instead treated as made for the following tax year. This is one federal rule; no additional independent source was found restating this specific deadline separately.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 1362(b)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, S corporation election timing
citations.quote: An election under subsection (a) may be made by a small business corporation for any taxable year— (A) at any time during the preceding taxable year, or (B) at any time during the taxable year and on or before the 15th day of the 3d month of the taxable year.

clauses.title: Revoking the Election
clauses.body: Unlike making the election in the first place, which requires every shareholder's consent, revoking it takes less: shareholders holding more than half of {{companyName}}'s shares, as of the day the revocation is made, is enough to consent to revoke. Timing controls when it takes effect: a revocation made by the 15th day of the third month of the tax year is effective retroactively to the start of that same tax year; made any later, it's effective starting the following tax year instead — unless the revocation itself specifies a later, prospective effective date, in which case that specified date controls.
clauses.gap: This is one federal rule, verified against the current U.S. Code text. This asymmetry is real and worth noticing: unanimous consent is required to elect S status, but only a bare majority is required to end it — a minority shareholder who wants to keep S status has no statutory veto over a majority's decision to revoke it.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 1362(d)(1)(B) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, revocation requires more than half of shares, not unanimity
citations.quote: An election may be revoked only if shareholders holding more than one-half of the shares of stock of the corporation on the day on which the revocation is made consent to the revocation.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 1362(d)(1)(C) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, when a revocation takes effect
citations.quote: a revocation made during the taxable year and on or before the 15th day of the 3d month thereof shall be effective on the 1st day of such taxable year, and (ii) a revocation made during the taxable year but after such 15th day shall be effective on the 1st day of the following taxable year.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 1362(d)(1)(D) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, a revocation may instead specify a prospective date
citations.quote: If the revocation specifies a date for revocation which is on or after the day on which the revocation is made, the revocation shall be effective on and after the date so specified.

clauses.title: An Involuntary Termination Trap
clauses.body: S status can also end without anyone voting to end it. If {{companyName}} has accumulated earnings and profits (which generally means it was previously a C corporation, or acquired one, and never distributed out its retained C-corporation earnings) at the close of each of three consecutive tax years, and more than 25% of its gross receipts in each of those same three years comes from passive investment income — royalties, rents, dividends, interest, and annuities — the S election terminates automatically, effective the first day of the tax year after that third consecutive year.
clauses.gap: This is one federal rule, verified against the current U.S. Code text. This trap doesn't apply to an S corporation that has never had C-corporation earnings and profits to begin with — a company that has been an S corporation from its first tax year, and has no accumulated E&P from before that election, can't trigger this specific termination path no matter how passive its income is.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 1362(d)(3)(A) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, automatic termination for excess passive income with accumulated earnings and profits
citations.quote: An election under subsection (a) shall be terminated whenever the corporation— (I) has accumulated earnings and profits at the close of each of 3 consecutive taxable years, and (II) has gross receipts for each of such taxable years more than 25 percent of which are passive investment income.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 1362(d)(3)(A)(ii) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, when this termination becomes effective
citations.quote: Any termination under this paragraph shall be effective on and after the first day of the first taxable year beginning after the third consecutive taxable year referred to in clause (i).

clauses.title: If S Status Ends — Fixing It or Waiting It Out
clauses.body: If S status is lost — whether by revocation, by ceasing to qualify, or by the passive-income trap above — two different paths exist depending on the cause. If the loss happened by genuine accident (a missed shareholder consent, an eligibility slip the corporation didn't realize), the IRS can treat the corporation as having remained an S corporation the whole time, if it determines the circumstances were inadvertent, the corporation fixes the underlying problem within a reasonable time after discovering it, and the corporation and every affected shareholder agree to make whatever tax adjustments the IRS requires. Absent that relief, once an election has been terminated, the corporation generally can't re-elect S status again until its fifth tax year after the one the termination took effect in — a five-year wait — unless the IRS consents to an earlier re-election.
clauses.gap: This is one federal rule, verified against the current U.S. Code text. Inadvertent-termination relief is a determination the IRS makes on the specific facts, not something a corporation can grant itself by simply asserting good faith; this document doesn't state what the IRS actually looks for in making that determination.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 1362(f)(2) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, inadvertent termination relief — the IRS's determination
citations.quote: the Secretary determines that the circumstances resulting in such ineffectiveness or termination were inadvertent

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 1362(f)(3) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, inadvertent termination relief — fixing the problem
citations.quote: no later than a reasonable period of time after discovery of the circumstances resulting in such ineffectiveness or termination, steps were taken— (A) so that the corporation for which the election was made or the termination occurred is a small business corporation or a qualified subchapter S subsidiary, as the case may be, or (B) to acquire the required shareholder consents

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 1362(f)(4) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, inadvertent termination relief — shareholder agreement to adjustments
citations.quote: the corporation for which the election was made or the termination occurred, and each person who was a shareholder in such corporation at any time during the period specified pursuant to this subsection, agrees to make such adjustments (consistent with the treatment of such corporation as an S corporation or a qualified subchapter S subsidiary, as the case may be) as may be required by the Secretary with respect to such period

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 1362(f) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, inadvertent termination relief — the actual outcome
citations.quote: then, notwithstanding the circumstances resulting in such ineffectiveness or termination, such corporation shall be treated as an S corporation or a qualified subchapter S subsidiary, as the case may be, during the period specified by the Secretary.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 1362(g) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, the five-year bar on re-electing after termination
citations.quote: such corporation (and any successor corporation) shall not be eligible to make an election under subsection (a) for any taxable year before its 5th taxable year which begins after the 1st taxable year for which such termination is effective, unless the Secretary consents to such election.

clauses.title: How to File
clauses.body: The election is made by filing IRS Form 2553, signed by an authorized corporate officer, with the shareholder consents required above attached or included on the form. Form 2553 is filed with the IRS — it is a federal tax filing, not a state filing, and it doesn't replace or change anything filed with {{companyName}}'s state of incorporation or organization.

clauses.title: Purpose
clauses.body: This agreement restricts the transfer of ownership interests in {{companyName}} and sets out what happens to an owner's interest when a triggering event occurs, so the remaining owners and the departing owner's interest don't end up governed only by whatever the default rule happens to be.

clauses.title: Triggering Events
clauses.body:
This agreement applies when any of the following happens to an owner:

☐ Death
☐ Permanent disability
☐ Divorce or legal separation affecting ownership of the interest
☐ Voluntary withdrawal or resignation
☐ Involuntary termination or expulsion (as permitted by the company's governing documents)
☐ Bankruptcy or insolvency
☐ A bona fide offer from an outside buyer the owner wishes to accept
☐ Other: _______________________________________________

clauses.title: Right of First Refusal
clauses.body: Before an owner may transfer an interest to anyone outside the company in response to an outside offer, the owner must first offer that interest to {{companyName}} and then to the other owners, on the same price and terms as the outside offer. The company and the other owners have _______ days to accept the offer before the owner may proceed with the outside transfer.

clauses.title: Why This Matters for an LLC
clauses.body: Without an agreement like this one, a transfer of an LLC membership interest — by sale, gift, or on an owner's death — doesn't by itself dissolve the company or give the person who receives the interest a vote or a role in managing it. That person generally only receives the right to whatever distributions the original owner would have received.
clauses.gap: This is one state's default rule, used here as real evidence of what happens automatically if the company's own governing documents don't set a different rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific company. This default cuts both ways: it's reassuring in that an unplanned transfer doesn't hand a stranger a vote, but it also means the remaining owners can end up running the business alongside someone who has an economic stake but no say and no obligation to contribute, unless this agreement — or the operating agreement itself — sets up a mechanism to convert that situation into an actual buyout.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17705.02(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, effect of a transfer
citations.quote: A transfer does not by itself cause a member’s dissociation or a dissolution and winding up of the activities of a limited liability company.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17705.02(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, a transferee doesn't get management rights
citations.quote: a transfer does not entitle the transferee to do any of the following: (A) Vote or otherwise participate in the management or conduct of the activities of a limited liability company.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17705.02(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, a transferee's economic rights
citations.quote: A transferee has the right to receive, in accordance with the transfer, distributions to which the transferor would otherwise be entitled

clauses.title: Making the Restriction Stick for an LLC
clauses.body: For this restriction to actually bind an outside buyer or an owner's heirs — not just the owners who signed it — it needs to be written into {{companyName}}'s operating agreement, not left as a side agreement. A transfer that violates a restriction written into the operating agreement is ineffective against anyone who had notice of the restriction at the time of the transfer. The company also doesn't have to give effect to a transferee's rights under that same statute until it has actual notice that the transfer happened.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine mechanism — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC. The practical implication: a right of first refusal that lives only in this standalone agreement, and isn't also incorporated into the operating agreement itself, may not bind a transferee who never saw this agreement and had no notice of it. This document is meant to work alongside the operating agreement, not replace it.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17705.02(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, a transfer restriction binds a transferee with notice
citations.quote: A transfer of a transferable interest in violation of a restriction on transfer contained in the operating agreement is ineffective as to a person having notice of the restriction at the time of transfer.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17705.02(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, the company need not recognize a transfer without notice
citations.quote: A limited liability company need not give effect to a transferee’s rights under this section until the limited liability company has notice of the transfer.

clauses.title: Why This Matters for a Corporation
clauses.body: If {{companyName}} is a corporation, this transfer restriction only binds someone who buys or receives shares without knowing about it if the restriction is noted conspicuously on the stock certificate or the written statement that takes its place.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine formal requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. A transfer restriction that exists only in this agreement or the bylaws, without also appearing on the actual shares or share records, risks being unenforceable against someone who buys or receives those shares without actual knowledge of the restriction.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 418(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, required disclosure of a transfer restriction
citations.quote: The fact that the shares are subject to restrictions upon transfer.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 418(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, enforceability against a transferee without notice
citations.quote: Unless stated on the certificate, the initial transaction statement, and written statements as required by subdivision (a), no restriction upon transfer, no right of redemption and no voting agreement under subdivision (a) of Section 706, no irrevocable proxy under subdivision (e) of Section 705, and no voting restriction imposed by the corporation shall be enforceable against a transferee of the shares without actual knowledge of such restriction, right, agreement or proxy.

clauses.title: If the Corporation Is a Close Corporation
clauses.body: If {{companyName}} has formally elected close corporation status, there's a separate, stricter rule beyond the general transfer-restriction disclosure above: a close corporation's shares must carry a specific legend on their face capping the number of shareholders of record (a number the corporation sets, up to a statutory maximum), and any voluntary transfer that would push the shareholder count past that cap is void — not just unenforceable against an unknowing buyer, but void outright.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine formal requirement for a specific corporate subtype — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, and it only applies if the corporation has actually elected close corporation status, which most small corporations have not; whether that election was made is stated in the corporation's own articles of incorporation.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 418(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, required close-corporation legend and shareholder cap
citations.quote: All certificates representing shares of a close corporation shall contain in addition to any other statements required by this section, the following conspicuous legend on the face thereof: “This corporation is a close corporation. The number of holders of record of its shares of all classes cannot exceed ____ [a number not in excess of 35]. Any attempted voluntary inter vivos transfer which would violate this requirement is void. Refer to the articles, bylaws and any agreements on file with the secretary of the corporation for further restrictions.”

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 418(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, a transfer past the cap is void
citations.quote: Any attempted voluntary inter vivos transfer of the shares of a close corporation which would result in the number of holders of record of its shares exceeding the maximum number specified in its articles is void if the certificate contains the legend required by subdivision (c).

clauses.title: Parties and Property
clauses.body: This is a residential lease agreement between {{landlordName}} ("Landlord") and {{tenantName}} ("Tenant") for the property at {{propertyAddress}}. The lease term runs from {{leaseStartDate}} to {{leaseEndDate}}.

clauses.title: Rent
clauses.body: Tenant will pay Landlord rent of ${{monthlyRent}} per month, due on the _______ day of each month, payable by: _______________________________________________.

clauses.title: Security Deposit
clauses.body: Landlord may charge a security deposit of up to one month's rent, in addition to the first month's rent. If Landlord is an individual (or an LLC whose members are all individuals) who owns no more than two residential rental properties totaling no more than four units, Landlord may charge up to two months' rent instead — except that this higher cap doesn't apply if the prospective tenant is a service member, in which case the general one-month cap still controls. The deposit may only be used for: (1) unpaid rent; (2) repairing damage Tenant (or Tenant's guest) caused, beyond ordinary wear and tear; (3) cleaning needed to return the unit to the same level of cleanliness it was in when the tenancy began; and (4) remedying a future default in returning or restoring personal property, if the lease authorizes that use. Within 21 days after Tenant moves out, Landlord must give Tenant an itemized statement of any deductions and return the remaining deposit.
clauses.gap: A lease of six months or longer can separately require an advance rent payment of up to six months' rent, on top of the security deposit cap above — a different rule from the deposit cap itself, and easy to conflate with it. This is one state's statute, current as of a 2024 change that lowered the general cap to one month's rent; deposit limits and return deadlines vary by state, and this document doesn't track any state but this one. All six citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1950.5) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, general security deposit cap
citations.quote: a landlord shall not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of an amount equal to one month’s rent, in addition to any rent for the first month paid on or before initial occupancy.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(c)(5)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, higher cap for a small individual landlord
citations.quote: a landlord shall not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of an amount equal to two months’ rent, in addition to any rent for the first month paid on or before initial occupancy if the landlord meets both of the following requirements: (i) The landlord is a natural person or a limited liability company in which all members are natural persons. (ii) The landlord owns no more than two residential rental properties that collectively include no more than four dwelling units offered for rent.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(c)(5)(B) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the small-landlord cap doesn't apply to a service-member tenant
citations.quote: Subparagraph (A) shall not apply if the prospective tenant is a service member.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(c)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, advance rent for a longer lease
citations.quote: This subdivision does not prohibit an advance payment of not less than six months’ rent if the term of the lease is six months or longer.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the four permitted uses of a security deposit
citations.quote: (1) The compensation of a landlord for a tenant’s default in the payment of rent. (2) The repair of damages to the premises, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear, caused by the tenant or by a guest or licensee of the tenant. (3) The cleaning of the premises upon termination of the tenancy necessary to return the unit to the same level of cleanliness it was in at the inception of the tenancy.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(b)(4) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the fourth permitted use — future personal-property defaults
citations.quote: (4) To remedy future defaults by the tenant in any obligation under the rental agreement to restore, replace, or return personal property or appurtenances, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear, if the security deposit is authorized to be applied thereto by the rental agreement.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(h)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, deposit return deadline
citations.quote: No later than 21 calendar days after the tenant has vacated the premises

clauses.title: Tenant's Right to a Pre-Move-Out Inspection
clauses.body: Before Tenant moves out, Landlord must notify Tenant in writing of Tenant's option to request an initial (pre-move-out) inspection and the right to be present for it. If Tenant requests one, Landlord must inspect no earlier than two weeks before the move-out date and give Tenant at least 48 hours' written notice of the inspection date and time. The point of this inspection is to let Tenant fix any identified problems before move-out, to avoid a deduction from the deposit for them.
clauses.gap: If Tenant requests this inspection and the unit isn't full of Tenant's belongings in a way that would hide problems from view, Landlord generally can't later deduct from the deposit for a repair or cleaning issue that wasn't identified at that inspection. This is a real, concrete consequence of the inspection right, not just a formality — and it's easy to miss because the inspection itself is optional (Tenant has to request it; if Tenant doesn't, this whole process — and its protection — doesn't apply). This entire inspection right doesn't apply at all if the tenancy is ending through an unlawful detainer based on nonpayment of rent, a lease breach, or waste/nuisance — those specific for-cause terminations void the right described in this clause. This is one state's statute; not every state gives tenants this specific right. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1950.5) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(f)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the pre-move-out inspection right
citations.quote: Within a reasonable time after notification of either party’s intention to terminate the tenancy, or before the end of the lease term, the landlord shall notify the tenant in writing of the tenant’s option to request an initial inspection and of the tenant’s right to be present at the inspection. At a reasonable time, but no earlier than two weeks before the termination or the end of lease date, the landlord, or an agent of the landlord, shall, upon the request of the tenant, make an initial inspection of the premises prior to any final inspection the landlord makes after the tenant has vacated the premises. The purpose of the initial inspection shall be to allow the tenant an opportunity to remedy identified deficiencies, in a manner consistent with the rights and obligations of the parties under the rental agreement, in order to avoid deductions from the security.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(f)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, 48-hour inspection notice
citations.quote: The landlord shall give at least 48 hours’ prior written notice of the date and time of the inspection if either a mutual time is agreed upon, or if a mutually agreed time cannot be scheduled but the tenant still wishes an inspection.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(f)(4) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, effect of not identifying an issue at the inspection
citations.quote: if an initial inspection is conducted pursuant to this subdivision and, at the time of inspection, the premises do not contain tenant possessions that prevent the landlord from identifying repairs or cleanings due to the presence of those possessions, the landlord shall not use the security for deductions for repairs or cleanings that are not identified in the itemized statement described in paragraph (2).

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(f)(7) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, this right doesn't apply to a for-cause unlawful detainer
citations.quote: The requirements of this subdivision do not apply when the tenancy is terminated pursuant to subdivision (2), (3), or (4) of Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

clauses.title: Photo Documentation Requirement
clauses.body: For a tenancy that begins on or after July 1, 2025, Landlord must photograph the unit before or at the start of the tenancy. Separately, beginning April 1, 2025, Landlord must photograph the unit after Tenant moves out but before making any repairs or cleaning charged against the deposit, and again after that repair or cleaning is finished.
clauses.gap: This is a very recent requirement — it phases in on two different dates for two different purposes (a baseline record at move-in, and a before-and-after record around any move-out deduction) — and it's one state's statute, not a nationwide practice. The move-out photos aren't just good practice: for any deduction the landlord makes for repairs or cleaning, the statute separately requires the landlord to provide those same photographs to the tenant, along with a written explanation of the cost, as part of the itemized deduction statement — so skipping the photos leaves the landlord unable to fully comply with that separate documentation requirement. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1950.5) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(g)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, move-in photo requirement
citations.quote: For tenancies that begin on or after July 1, 2025, the landlord shall take photographs of the unit immediately before, or at the inception of, the tenancy.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(g)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, move-out before-and-after photo requirement
citations.quote: Beginning April 1, 2025, the landlord shall take photographs of the unit within a reasonable time after the possession of the unit is returned to the landlord, but prior to any repairs or cleanings for which the landlord will make a deduction from or claim against the security deposit pursuant to this section, and shall also take photographs of the unit within a reasonable time after such repairs or cleanings are completed.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(h)(2)(D) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the photos are a required part of the deduction documentation
citations.quote: If a deduction is made for repairs or cleanings allowed by this section, the landlord shall provide photographs taken pursuant to subdivision (g), along with a written explanation of the cost of the allowable repairs or cleanings, as described in subparagraphs (A) to (C), inclusive.

clauses.title: Habitability
clauses.body: Landlord must maintain the property in a condition fit for human habitation and repair conditions that make it uninhabitable, except for conditions Tenant caused.
clauses.gap: The statute's own text says this duty applies "in the absence of an agreement to the contrary" — which could read as if a lease could waive it. A separate provision closes that door for residential tenancies: a lease clause waiving or modifying this duty is void as against public policy, for any condition that actually makes the unit uninhabitable. The one thing landlord and tenant can agree to instead is having the tenant handle some repairs or maintenance as part of the rental terms — that's different from waiving the underlying habitability duty altogether. This is one state's statute; habitability protections exist in some form in most states, but the details vary.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1941 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, landlord's habitability duty
citations.quote: The lessor of a building intended for the occupation of human beings must, in the absence of an agreement to the contrary, put it into a condition fit for such occupation, and repair all subsequent dilapidations thereof, which render it untenantable, except such as are mentioned in section nineteen hundred and twenty-nine.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1942.1 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, habitability duty can't be waived
citations.quote: Any agreement by a lessee of a dwelling waiving or modifying his rights under Section 1941 or 1942 shall be void as contrary to public policy with respect to any condition which renders the premises untenantable, except that the lessor and the lessee may agree that the lessee shall undertake to improve, repair or maintain all or stipulated portions of the dwelling as part of the consideration for rental.

clauses.title: What "Habitable" Specifically Means
clauses.body: A unit is legally uninhabitable if it substantially lacks any of the following: effective weatherproofing (including intact windows and doors); working plumbing and gas fixtures that met the code in effect when installed; hot and cold running water connected to an approved sewage system; working heating that met the code in effect when installed; working electrical wiring and lighting that met the code in effect when installed; a building and grounds kept clean, sanitary, and free of debris, rodents, and vermin; adequate garbage and rubbish receptacles, kept in clean condition and good repair; and floors, stairways, and railings kept in good repair.
clauses.gap: This is the specific legal checklist behind the general "habitable" duty stated above — a unit can look fine and still be legally uninhabitable if it's substantially missing even one of these items. This list also includes a locking mail receptacle requirement for residential hotel units specifically, which this document doesn't restate since it isn't relevant to an ordinary residential lease. This is one state's statute; other states define habitability differently, whether by statute, regulation, or case law. This is a single statutory subsection; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1941.1(a)(1)-(8) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the specific tenantability checklist
citations.quote: A dwelling shall be deemed untenantable for purposes of Section 1941 if it substantially lacks any of the following affirmative standard characteristics or is a residential unit described in Section 17920.3 or 17920.10 of the Health and Safety Code: (1) Effective waterproofing and weather protection of roof and exterior walls, including unbroken windows and doors. (2) Plumbing or gas facilities that conformed to applicable law in effect at the time of installation, maintained in good working order. (3) A water supply approved under applicable law that is under the control of the tenant, capable of producing hot and cold running water, or a system that is under the control of the landlord, that produces hot and cold running water, furnished to appropriate fixtures, and connected to a sewage disposal system approved under applicable law. (4) Heating facilities that conformed with applicable law at the time of installation, maintained in good working order. (5) Electrical lighting, with wiring and electrical equipment that conformed with applicable law at the time of installation, maintained in good working order. (6) Building, grounds, and appurtenances at the time of the commencement of the lease or rental agreement, and all areas under control of the landlord, kept in every part clean, sanitary, and free from all accumulations of debris, filth, rubbish, garbage, rodents, and vermin. (7) An adequate number of appropriate receptacles for garbage and rubbish, in clean condition and good repair at the time of the commencement of the lease or rental agreement, with the landlord providing appropriate serviceable receptacles thereafter and being responsible for the clean condition and good repair of the receptacles under their control. (8) Floors, stairways, and railings maintained in good repair.

clauses.title: Stove and Refrigerator Requirement
clauses.body: For a lease entered into, amended, or extended on or after January 1, 2026, a unit is also legally uninhabitable if it substantially lacks a working stove capable of safely generating heat for cooking, or a working refrigerator capable of safely storing food — and a stove or refrigerator under an active manufacturer or public-entity recall doesn't count as safe. Tenant and Landlord can agree at signing that Tenant will bring and maintain their own refrigerator instead, using specific statutory language, but Tenant can end that arrangement with 30 days' written notice, after which Landlord must install a working refrigerator.
clauses.gap: This requirement doesn't apply to every kind of housing — it's carved out for permanent supportive housing, single-room-occupancy units, residential hotel units, and housing with shared or communal kitchens (including assisted living facilities), since those housing types often don't work the way an ordinary rental unit does. This is a very new requirement — it only applies to leases entered into, amended, or extended on or after January 1, 2026 — and it's one state's statute, not a general rule. All four citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1941.1) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1941.1(a)(10) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, stove requirement
citations.quote: a stove that is maintained in good working order and capable of safely generating heat for cooking purposes. A stove that is subject to a recall by the manufacturer or a public entity is not capable of safely generating heat for cooking purposes. This paragraph shall only apply to a lease entered into, amended, or extended on or after January 1, 2026.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1941.1(a)(11)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, refrigerator requirement
citations.quote: a refrigerator that is maintained in good working order and capable of safely storing food. A refrigerator that is subject to recall by the manufacturer or a public entity is not capable of safely storing food.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1941.1(a)(11)(B)(i) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, required opt-out language for a tenant-supplied refrigerator
citations.quote: The lease contains a statement in substantially the following form: “Under state law, the landlord is required to provide a refrigerator in good working order in your unit. By checking this box, you acknowledge that you have asked to bring your own refrigerator and that you are responsible for keeping that refrigerator in working order.”

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1941.1(a)(11)(B)(ii) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, tenant's right to revert to a landlord-provided refrigerator
citations.quote: The lease provides that the tenant may, with 30 days written notice, inform the landlord that they no longer wish to keep their own refrigerator in the unit, and that at the end of the 30-day notice period, the landlord shall install a refrigerator in good working order in the unit.

clauses.title: Landlord's Right to Enter
clauses.body: Landlord may enter the unit only in these specific cases: (1) an emergency; (2) to make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations, or improvements, to supply necessary or agreed services, or to show the unit to a prospective or actual purchaser, mortgagee, tenant, worker, or contractor, or to make the pre-move-out inspection described elsewhere in this document; (3) when Tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit; or (4) under a court order. (Two further categories exist under separate statutes for specific health, safety, and emergency-preparedness purposes this document doesn't cover.) Except in an emergency or abandonment, entry is limited to normal business hours and generally requires reasonable written notice stating the date, approximate time, and purpose of the entry — but written notice itself isn't always required: no notice at all is required if Tenant is present and consents to the entry at the time of entry; oral notice is enough to show the unit to a prospective or actual purchaser, if Landlord has separately given Tenant written notice within the last 120 days that the property is for sale; and Landlord and Tenant may agree orally to a repair or service visit within the coming week, with no written notice required for that agreed visit either. Landlord can't abuse this right of access or use it to harass Tenant.
clauses.gap: Twenty-four hours' written notice is presumed reasonable, but that's a presumption, not an absolute floor — it can be rebutted by evidence either way. This is one state's statute; notice requirements for landlord entry vary by state. All citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1954) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the specific permitted purposes for entry
citations.quote: A landlord may enter the dwelling unit only in the following cases: (1) In case of emergency. (2) To make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations or improvements, supply necessary or agreed services, or exhibit the dwelling unit to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, workers, or contractors or to make an inspection pursuant to subdivision (f) of Section 1950.5. (3) When the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the premises. (4) Pursuant to court order.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, entry limited to normal business hours
citations.quote: Except in cases of emergency or when the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the premises, entry may not be made during other than normal business hours unless the tenant consents to an entry during other than normal business hours at the time of entry.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, written notice requirement
citations.quote: Except as provided in subdivision (e), or as provided in paragraph (2) or (3), the landlord shall give the tenant reasonable notice in writing of his or her intent to enter and enter only during normal business hours. The notice shall include the date, approximate time, and purpose of the entry.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, 24-hour presumption
citations.quote: Twenty-four hours shall be presumed to be reasonable notice in absence of evidence to the contrary.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(d)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, oral notice suffices to show the unit to a prospective purchaser
citations.quote: If the purpose of the entry is to exhibit the dwelling unit to prospective or actual purchasers, the notice may be given orally, in person or by telephone, if the landlord or his or her agent has notified the tenant in writing within 120 days of the oral notice that the property is for sale and that the landlord or agent may contact the tenant orally for the purpose described above.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(d)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, an oral agreement for a repair or service visit needs no written notice
citations.quote: The tenant and the landlord may agree orally to an entry to make agreed repairs or supply agreed services. The agreement shall include the date and approximate time of the entry, which shall be within one week of the agreement. In this case, the landlord is not required to provide the tenant a written notice.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, when no notice at all is required
citations.quote: No notice of entry is required under this section: (1) To respond to an emergency. (2) If the tenant is present and consents to the entry at the time of entry. (3) After the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, no abuse or harassment
citations.quote: The landlord may not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant.

clauses.title: Tenant's Maintenance Responsibilities
clauses.body: Tenant will keep the unit clean and sanitary, use all appliances and fixtures properly, and promptly notify Landlord of any condition needing repair. Tenant is responsible for damage caused by Tenant's own negligence or misuse, beyond ordinary wear and tear.

clauses.title: Late Fees
clauses.body: If rent is not paid within _______ days of the due date, Tenant will owe a late fee of $_______ (or _______% of the monthly rent).

clauses.title: Declaration
clauses.body: I, {{testatorName}}, a resident of {{testatorCounty}} County, California, declare this to be my Last Will and Testament, and I revoke all prior wills and codicils I have made.

clauses.title: Testamentary Capacity
clauses.body: For this will to be valid, {{testatorName}} must have testamentary capacity at the time it's signed: sufficient mental capacity to understand that this is a will, to understand and recall the nature and extent of {{testatorName}}'s own property, and to remember and understand {{testatorName}}'s relationships with living family members and others affected by the will. Capacity can also be defeated a second way, independent of the general test: a mental health disorder involving delusions or hallucinations that actually caused a specific distribution decision the testator wouldn't otherwise have made.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual legal test for capacity — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will. The two paths to incapacity are independent: a testator can meet the general understand-and-recall test yet still have a specific gift invalidated if it's shown to be the product of a delusion, and this statute doesn't override other evidence rules already used to prove incapacity generally. A conservator can make a will for a conservatee only with specific prior court authorization — this document doesn't cover that separate process.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6100.5(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the two-part testamentary capacity test
citations.quote: An individual is not mentally competent to make a will if, at the time of making the will, either of the following is true: (1) The individual does not have sufficient mental capacity to be able to do any of the following: (A) Understand the nature of the testamentary act. (B) Understand and recollect the nature and situation of the individual’s property. (C) Remember and understand the individual’s relations to living descendants, spouse, and parents, and those whose interests are affected by the will. (2) The individual suffers from a mental health disorder with symptoms including delusions or hallucinations, which delusions or hallucinations result in the individual’s devising property in a way that, except for the existence of the delusions or hallucinations, the individual would not have done.

clauses.title: How This Will Must Be Signed
