clauses.body: For this will to be valid, it must be signed by {{testatorName}} (or by someone else in {{testatorName}}'s presence and at {{testatorName}}'s direction), and witnessed by at least two people who are present at the same time, who each watch {{testatorName}} sign or acknowledge the will, and who understand that what they're signing is {{testatorName}}'s will.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual execution requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will. A will that misses one of these formalities isn't automatically void: if the person offering the will can show by clear and convincing evidence that the testator intended the document to be their will at the time they signed it, the will can still be treated as validly executed. That's a real, but demanding, safety net — clear and convincing evidence is a higher bar than the ordinary preponderance standard used in most civil disputes. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 6110) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6110(b)-(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, signature and witness requirements
citations.quote: The will shall be signed by one of the following: (1) By the testator. (2) In the testator’s name by some other person in the testator’s presence and by the testator’s direction. (3) By a conservator pursuant to a court order to make a will under Section 2580. (c) (1) Except as provided in paragraph (2), the will shall be witnessed by being signed, during the testator’s lifetime, by at least two persons each of whom (A) being present at the same time, witnessed either the signing of the will or the testator’s acknowledgment of the signature or of the will and (B) understand that the instrument they sign is the testator’s will.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6110(c)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the harmless-error exception for a defectively executed will
citations.quote: If a will was not executed in compliance with paragraph (1), the will shall be treated as if it was executed in compliance with that paragraph if the proponent of the will establishes by clear and convincing evidence that, at the time the testator signed the will, the testator intended the will to constitute the testator’s will.

clauses.title: The Handwritten-Will Alternative
clauses.body: A completely different kind of will exists under this same state's law: a will that doesn't meet the signature-and-witness requirements above can still be valid as a holographic will — with no witnesses required at all — if its signature and its material provisions are in the testator's own handwriting. A holographic will that doesn't state the date it was signed carries a real risk: if that missing date creates doubt about whether it or a different will controls, the undated holographic will loses to the other one unless it can be shown to have been signed later — and if there's a real question about whether the testator had capacity at some point during the possible window it was signed, the undated will is invalid unless it's shown to have been signed while the testator had capacity.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a lower-formality alternative genuinely exists — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will, and not a recommendation to use it instead of a properly witnessed will. This document is a witnessed will under the requirements described above, not a holographic one; this clause explains the alternative path for context, since a testator who later handwrites informal notes about their estate could unintentionally create a second, competing holographic will. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 6111) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6111(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, holographic will validity
citations.quote: A will that does not comply with Section 6110 is valid as a holographic will, whether or not witnessed, if the signature and the material provisions are in the handwriting of the testator.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6111(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the risk of an undated holographic will
citations.quote: If a holographic will does not contain a statement as to the date of its execution and: (1) If the omission results in doubt as to whether its provisions or the inconsistent provisions of another will are controlling, the holographic will is invalid to the extent of the inconsistency unless the time of its execution is established to be after the date of execution of the other will. (2) If it is established that the testator lacked testamentary capacity at any time during which the will might have been executed, the will is invalid unless it is established that it was executed at a time when the testator had testamentary capacity.

clauses.title: How This Will Can Be Revoked
clauses.body: {{testatorName}} can revoke this will, in whole or in part, in one of two ways: by a later will that revokes it expressly or by conflicting with it, or by burning, tearing, canceling, obliterating, or destroying it (personally, or by someone else in {{testatorName}}'s presence and at {{testatorName}}'s direction) with the specific intent of revoking it.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual, exclusive methods of revocation — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will. A physical act (burning, tearing, and so on) done accidentally, or by someone without the testator's direction, doesn't revoke a will — the intent to revoke is what matters, not just the physical damage. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 6120); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6120 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the two methods of revoking a will
citations.quote: A will or any part thereof is revoked by any of the following: (a) A subsequent will which revokes the prior will or part expressly or by inconsistency. (b) Being burned, torn, canceled, obliterated, or destroyed, with the intent and for the purpose of revoking it, by either (1) the testator or (2) another person in the testator’s presence and by the testator’s direction.

clauses.title: What a Later Divorce Does to This Will
clauses.body: If {{testatorName}}'s marriage is later dissolved or annulled, that alone automatically revokes — unless this will expressly says otherwise — any gift to the former spouse, any power of appointment given to the former spouse, and any nomination of the former spouse as executor, trustee, conservator, or guardian. Property that would have gone to the former spouse instead passes as though the former spouse died before {{testatorName}}. If {{testatorName}} later remarries the same former spouse, the revoked provisions come back into effect.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine, automatic default — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will. A legal separation that doesn't actually terminate marital status is not a "dissolution" for this purpose, so a will's provisions for a separated-but-still-married spouse aren't automatically revoked by a separation alone. No other change in circumstances — the birth of a child aside from the separate omitted-child protections, a falling out with a beneficiary, and so on — automatically revokes any part of a will under this statute; a testator who wants a different result has to actually update the will. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 6122) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6122(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, automatic revocation of former-spouse provisions on divorce
citations.quote: Unless the will expressly provides otherwise, if after executing a will the testator’s marriage is dissolved or annulled, the dissolution or annulment revokes all of the following: (1) Any disposition or appointment of property made by the will to the former spouse. (2) Any provision of the will conferring a general or special power of appointment on the former spouse. (3) Any provision of the will nominating the former spouse as executor, trustee, conservator, or guardian.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6122(b)-(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, revival on remarriage and treatment as predeceased
citations.quote: If any disposition or other provision of a will is revoked solely by this section, it is revived by the testator’s remarriage to the former spouse. (c) In case of revocation by dissolution or annulment: (1) Property prevented from passing to a former spouse because of the revocation passes as if the former spouse failed to survive the testator. (2) Other provisions of the will conferring some power or office on the former spouse shall be interpreted as if the former spouse failed to survive the testator.

clauses.title: A Spouse Married After This Will Was Signed
clauses.body: If {{testatorName}} marries someone after signing this will and never updates the will to provide for that spouse, the law doesn't simply let the omission stand — the omitted spouse is entitled by default to a share of the estate: half of the community and quasi-community property, plus a share of separate property equal to what the spouse would have received had there been no will at all, capped at half the separate property in the estate.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine, automatic protection — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will. This default share doesn't apply in several real situations: if the will itself shows the omission was intentional; if the testator provided for the new spouse outside the will (and meant that transfer to replace a provision in it); if the spouse signed a valid waiver of the right to share in the estate; or — a specific anti-abuse rule — if the spouse was the testator's paid care custodian, the marriage began while they were providing that care (or within 90 days after), and the testator died less than six months after the marriage, unless the spouse can prove by clear and convincing evidence that the marriage was genuine and not the result of undue influence, fraud, or duress. This document doesn't update itself to reflect a marriage after signing — a testator who marries after execution needs a new will or a codicil to actually provide for the new spouse, rather than relying on this default share.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21610 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the omitted spouse's default share
citations.quote: Except as provided in Section 21611, if a decedent fails to provide in a testamentary instrument for the decedent’s surviving spouse who married the decedent after the execution of all of the decedent’s testamentary instruments, the omitted spouse shall receive a share in the decedent’s estate, consisting of the following property in said estate: (a) The one-half of the community property that belongs to the decedent under Section 100. (b) The one-half of the quasi-community property that belongs to the decedent under Section 101. (c) A share of the separate property of the decedent equal in value to that which the spouse would have received if the decedent had died without having executed a testamentary instrument, but in no event is the share to be more than one-half the value of the separate property in the estate.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21611 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, when the omitted-spouse share doesn't apply
citations.quote: The spouse shall not receive a share of the estate under Section 21610 if any of the following is established: (a) The decedent’s failure to provide for the spouse in the decedent’s testamentary instruments was intentional and that intention appears from the testamentary instruments. (b) The decedent provided for the spouse by transfer outside of the estate passing by the decedent’s testamentary instruments and the intention that the transfer be in lieu of a provision in said instruments is shown by statements of the decedent or from the amount of the transfer or by other evidence. (c) The spouse made a valid agreement waiving the right to share in the decedent’s estate.

clauses.title: A Child Born or Adopted After This Will Was Signed
clauses.body: A child of {{testatorName}} who is born or adopted after this will is signed, and who isn't provided for in it, is entitled by default to a share of the estate equal to what that child would have received had there been no will at all. The same default share applies to a child alive when the will was signed whom {{testatorName}} left out only because {{testatorName}} believed the child was dead or didn't know about the child's birth.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine, automatic protection for an after-born or after-adopted child — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will. This document doesn't update itself to reflect a child born or adopted after signing; a testator who has, or expects to have, additional children after this will is executed should account for that here directly (for example, by defining "children" to include children born or adopted later) rather than relying on this default share, which is a fallback for an unaddressed gap, not a substitute for actually saying what the testator wants.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21620 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the omitted after-born or after-adopted child's default share
citations.quote: Except as provided in Section 21621, if a decedent fails to provide in a testamentary instrument for a child of decedent born or adopted after the execution of all of the decedent’s testamentary instruments, the omitted child shall receive a share in the decedent’s estate equal in value to that which the child would have received if the decedent had died without having executed any testamentary instrument.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21622 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, a child the testator believed dead or didn't know about
citations.quote: If, at the time of the execution of all of decedent’s testamentary instruments effective at the time of decedent’s death, the decedent failed to provide for a living child solely because the decedent believed the child to be dead or was unaware of the birth of the child, the child shall receive a share in the estate equal in value to that which the child would have received if the decedent had died without having executed any testamentary instruments.

clauses.title: If a Beneficiary Dies at Nearly the Same Time
clauses.body: Under this state's default rule, a beneficiary who doesn't outlive {{testatorName}} by at least 120 hours (five days) is treated as if they died before {{testatorName}} — so their gift passes as though they'd predeceased, not to their own estate.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine default survival requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will. The burden runs against survival: if it can't be established by clear and convincing evidence that someone survived by the full 120 hours, they're deemed not to have survived. There's a real exception: this 120-hour requirement doesn't apply if enforcing it would cause the property to escheat to the state for lack of any other heir. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 6403(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6403(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the 120-hour survival requirement
citations.quote: A person who fails to survive the decedent by 120 hours is deemed to have predeceased the decedent for the purpose of intestate succession, and the heirs are determined accordingly. If it cannot be established by clear and convincing evidence that a person who would otherwise be an heir has survived the decedent by 120 hours, it is deemed that the person failed to survive for the required period. The requirement of this section that a person who survives the decedent must survive the decedent by 120 hours does not apply if the application of the 120-hour survival requirement would result in the escheat of property to the state.

clauses.title: The Real Limits of a No-Contest Clause
clauses.body: A clause disinheriting anyone who challenges this will is far narrower than it sounds: under this state's law, a no-contest clause can only be enforced against a direct challenge to the will's validity brought without probable cause, and — only if the clause expressly says so — against a challenge to a property transfer on the ground that the property wasn't the testator's to give, or against filing or pursuing a creditor's claim. Probable cause exists if the facts known to the person challenging, at the time they filed, would lead a reasonable person to believe there's a reasonable likelihood the challenge will succeed after a chance to investigate further.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the real, narrow scope of no-contest enforcement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will, and not a claim about whether including such a clause is a good idea. A beneficiary who challenges a will in good faith, with a genuinely reasonable basis, isn't automatically disinherited just because the challenge ultimately fails — the probable-cause safe harbor protects a good-faith challenge regardless of outcome. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 21311) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21311(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the three narrow categories a no-contest clause can reach
citations.quote: A no contest clause shall only be enforced against the following types of contests: (1) A direct contest that is brought without probable cause. (2) A pleading to challenge a transfer of property on the grounds that it was not the transferor’s property at the time of the transfer. A no contest clause shall only be enforced under this paragraph if the no contest clause expressly provides for that application. (3) The filing of a creditor’s claim or prosecution of an action based on it. A no contest clause shall only be enforced under this paragraph if the no contest clause expressly provides for that application.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21311(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the definition of probable cause
citations.quote: For the purposes of this section, probable cause exists if, at the time of filing a contest, the facts known to the contestant would cause a reasonable person to believe that there is a reasonable likelihood that the requested relief will be granted after an opportunity for further investigation or discovery.

clauses.title: Nominating a Guardian for a Minor Child
clauses.body: {{testatorName}} can nominate a guardian of the person, the estate, or both, for a minor child in this will — but that nomination only actually controls in specific circumstances: either the other parent joins in or consents in writing to the same nominee, or, at the time a guardianship petition is actually filed, the other parent is dead, lacks the legal capacity to consent, or their consent wouldn't be required for the child to be adopted.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine legal mechanism — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific nomination, and not a guarantee that a court will follow it. A nomination in a will isn't self-executing — it takes effect only through an actual guardianship proceeding, and a court can still decline to appoint the nominee if doing so wouldn't serve the child's best interest. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 1500); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1500 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, when a parent's guardian nomination controls
citations.quote: Subject to Section 1502, a parent may nominate a guardian of the person or estate, or both, of a minor child in either of the following cases: (a) Where the other parent nominates, or consents in writing to the nomination of, the same guardian for the same child. (b) Where, at the time the petition for appointment of the guardian is filed, either (1) the other parent is dead or lacks legal capacity to consent to the nomination or (2) the consent of the other parent would not be required for an adoption of the child.

clauses.title: What Happens Without a Named Executor
clauses.body: This will names an executor below because naming one is what actually controls who administers {{testatorName}}'s estate. Absent that, or if the named executor can't or won't serve, state law sets a strict order of priority for who's entitled to be appointed instead — starting with a surviving spouse or domestic partner, then children, then more distant relatives, and eventually creditors or any other person, well down the list.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual statutory fallback — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate. This priority order is exactly why naming an executor (and at least one alternate) matters even for a modest estate: without it, administration defaults to whoever is next in this statutory line, which may not be the person the testator would have chosen. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 8461); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8461 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the statutory priority order for appointment as personal representative
citations.quote: Subject to the provisions of this article, a person in the following relation to the decedent is entitled to appointment as administrator in the following order of priority: (a) Surviving spouse or domestic partner as defined in Section 37. (b) Children. (c) Grandchildren. (d) Other issue. (e) Parents. (f) Brothers and sisters. (g) Issue of brothers and sisters. (h) Grandparents. (i) Issue of grandparents. (j) Children of a predeceased spouse or domestic partner. (k) Other issue of a predeceased spouse or domestic partner. (l) Other next of kin. (m) Parents of a predeceased spouse or domestic partner. (n) Issue of parents of a predeceased spouse or domestic partner. (o) Conservator or guardian of the estate acting in that capacity at the time of death who has filed a first account and is not acting as conservator or guardian for any other person. (p) Public administrator. (q) Creditors. (r) Any other person.

clauses.title: Bond Requirement — and How to Waive It
clauses.body: Unless waived, state law requires an appointed executor to post a bond — approved by the court, and conditioned on faithfully carrying out the job — before the court will actually issue them the authority to act. This will waives that requirement, which the law specifically allows a will to do; without a waiver in the will (or a written waiver signed by every beneficiary), the executor has to post one.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine default requirement and a genuine waiver mechanism — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate. A waiver in the will isn't absolute: a court can still require a bond anyway, on request or on its own motion, for good cause — so an executor shouldn't assume a waiver in this document guarantees no bond will ever be required. Both citations below are from different statutory sections (§ 8480 and § 8481), each supporting a distinct part of this claim.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8480 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the default bond requirement
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided by statute, every person appointed as personal representative shall, before letters are issued, give a bond approved by the court.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8481 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, how the bond requirement is waived
citations.quote: A bond is not required in either of the following cases: (1) The will waives the requirement of a bond. (2) All beneficiaries waive in writing the requirement of a bond and the written waivers are attached to the petition for appointment of a personal representative. This paragraph does not apply if the will requires a bond.

clauses.title: Proving This Will Later, Without a Fight
clauses.body: If this will isn't contested, state law makes it easy to actually prove it in court years later: it can be proved on the testimony of just one of the two subscribing witnesses, not both, and that witness's evidence can be given by affidavit — with a copy of the will attached — rather than requiring them to appear in person.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine, low-friction proof mechanism — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will. This shortcut disappears entirely if the will is actually contested; it only applies to the routine case where no one is disputing that the will is genuine. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 8220); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8220 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, proving a will with one witness's affidavit
citations.quote: Unless there is a contest of a will: (a) The will may be proved on the evidence of one of the subscribing witnesses only, if the evidence shows that the will was executed in all particulars as prescribed by law. (b) Evidence of execution of a will may be received by an affidavit of a subscribing witness to which there is attached a photographic copy of the will, or by an affidavit in the original will that includes or incorporates the attestation clause.

clauses.title: Specific Gifts
clauses.body:
I give the following specific items or amounts to the following people or organizations:

_______________________________________________ to _______________________________________________
_______________________________________________ to _______________________________________________
(Add additional lines as needed.) If any of these named beneficiaries doesn't survive me by 120 hours, that gift instead becomes part of my residuary estate, described below, unless I've stated a different result above.

clauses.title: Residuary Estate
clauses.body: I give the rest of my estate — everything not specifically given above — to {{residuaryBeneficiary}}. If {{residuaryBeneficiary}} doesn't survive me by 120 hours, my residuary estate instead passes to: _______________________________________________.

clauses.title: Executor
clauses.body: I nominate {{executorName}} to serve as executor of this will. If {{executorName}} is unable or unwilling to serve, I nominate {{alternateExecutorName}} to serve instead. I waive the requirement that my executor post a bond.

clauses.title: Guardian for Minor Children
clauses.body: If I have a minor child at the time of my death and a guardian is needed, I nominate {{guardianName}} to serve as guardian of the person and estate of that child. If {{guardianName}} is unable or unwilling to serve, I nominate {{alternateGuardianName}} to serve instead.

clauses.title: Signatures
clauses.body:
I, {{testatorName}}, sign my name to this instrument this ____ day of ______________, 20____, and declare that I sign it willingly, that I execute it as my free and voluntary act, and that I am of the age of majority and under no constraint or undue influence.

Testator: _______________________ Date: _______________

The foregoing instrument was signed, declared, and acknowledged by the testator, in our presence, as the testator's will. We, in the testator's presence, and at the testator's request, and in the presence of each other, sign our names as witnesses, and each of us declares that we understand this to be the testator's will.

Witness: _______________________ Date: _______________ Address: _______________________
Witness: _______________________ Date: _______________ Address: _______________________

clauses.title: How a Power of Attorney Must Be Signed
clauses.body: California law treats a power of attorney as legally sufficient only if it contains the date of its execution, is signed by the principal (or by another adult in the principal's presence and at the principal's direction), and is either acknowledged before a notary public or signed by at least two qualifying witnesses. A witness must be an adult and must witness either the principal's signing of the document or the principal's acknowledgment of the signature; {{agentName}} may not serve as a witness to {{principalName}}'s power of attorney.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how a power of attorney's execution formalities work under one representative state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs the execution of a specific power of attorney. Formality requirements (notary vs. witnesses, witness qualifications) vary by state.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4121 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: legal sufficiency requirements: date, signature, notarization or two witnesses
citations.quote: A power of attorney is legally sufficient if all of the following requirements are satisfied: (a) The power of attorney contains the date of its execution. (b) The power of attorney is signed either (1) by the principal or (2) in the principal's name by another adult in the principal's presence and at the principal's direction. (c) The power of attorney is either (1) acknowledged before a notary public or (2) signed by at least two witnesses who satisfy the requirements of Section 4122.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4122 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: witness qualifications
citations.quote: If the power of attorney is signed by witnesses, as provided in Section 4121, the following requirements shall be satisfied: (a) The witnesses shall be adults. (b) The attorney-in-fact may not act as a witness. (c) Each witness signing the power of attorney shall witness either the signing of the instrument by the principal or the principal's acknowledgment of the signature or the power of attorney.

clauses.title: Durability — Surviving the Principal's Incapacity
clauses.body: A power of attorney is not automatically revoked by {{principalName}}'s later incapacity if the document itself says so — either by stating that it "shall not be affected by subsequent incapacity of the principal," or by similar words showing that intent. Acts an agent takes under a durable power of attorney during a period of the principal's incapacity have the same legal effect, and bind {{principalName}} and {{principalName}}'s successors in interest, as if {{principalName}} had full capacity at the time.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how durability provisions function under one representative state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific power of attorney. Whether a power of attorney is durable by default, or only by express language, differs by state.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4124 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: durability requires specific language in the document
citations.quote: A durable power of attorney is a power of attorney by which a principal designates another person as attorney-in-fact in writing and the power of attorney contains any of the following statements: (a) "This power of attorney shall not be affected by subsequent incapacity of the principal." ... (c) Similar words showing the intent of the principal that the authority conferred shall be exercisable notwithstanding the principal's subsequent incapacity.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4125 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: acts during incapacity bind the principal
citations.quote: All acts done by an attorney-in-fact pursuant to a durable power of attorney during any period of incapacity of the principal have the same effect and inure to the benefit of and bind the principal and the principal's successors in interest as if the principal had capacity.

clauses.title: Immediate vs. Springing Effectiveness
clauses.body: A power of attorney's document can state that it becomes effective immediately upon signing, or instead state that it becomes effective only upon a later event — most commonly, {{principalName}}'s incapacity ("springing"). Where a springing structure is used, {{principalName}} can designate one or more persons who determine, by a written declaration signed under penalty of perjury, that the triggering event or contingency (such as incapacity) has occurred; that designated person can be {{agentName}}, someone else, or several people acting jointly. Once that written declaration is executed, the power of attorney becomes effective, and a person may rely on it without liability, regardless of whether the specified event actually occurred.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how a springing power of attorney's triggering mechanism works under one representative state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific power of attorney. The named-person determination method described here is one mechanism this state's statute makes available; it states elsewhere that it is not the only way a document may condition its own effectiveness.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4124(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: statutory language for a springing (incapacity-triggered) power of attorney
citations.quote: "This power of attorney shall become effective upon the incapacity of the principal."

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4129 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: mechanism for determining a springing power of attorney's trigger
citations.quote: In a springing power of attorney, the principal may designate one or more persons who, by a written declaration under penalty of perjury, have the power to determine conclusively that the specified event or contingency has occurred. The principal may designate the attorney-in-fact or another person to perform this function, either alone or jointly with other persons. (b) A springing power of attorney containing the designation described in subdivision (a) becomes effective when the person or persons designated in the power of attorney execute a written declaration under penalty of perjury that the specified event or contingency has occurred, and any person may act in reliance on the written declaration without liability to the principal or to any other person, regardless of whether the specified event or contingency has actually occurred.

clauses.title: The Agent's Core Fiduciary Duties
clauses.body: An agent acting under a power of attorney has a duty to act solely in {{principalName}}'s interest and to avoid conflicts of interest; an agent does not violate that duty solely by also personally benefiting from acting for {{principalName}}, or by having some conflicting interest in the property, care, or affairs involved. Separately, an agent has a duty to keep records of every transaction entered into on {{principalName}}'s behalf, though the duty to render an accounting of those records arises only in specific circumstances — such as when {{principalName}} requests it, the document itself requires it, a court orders it, or (after {{principalName}}'s death) the request comes from {{principalName}}'s personal representative or successor in interest.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the fiduciary duties an agent owes under a power of attorney under one representative state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific power of attorney. The precise content and triggers of these duties vary by state.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4232 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: duty of loyalty / avoiding conflicts of interest
citations.quote: An attorney-in-fact has a duty to act solely in the interest of the principal and to avoid conflicts of interest. (b) An attorney-in-fact is not in violation of the duty provided in subdivision (a) solely because the attorney-in-fact also benefits from acting for the principal, has conflicting interests in relation to the property, care, or affairs of the principal, or acts in an inconsistent manner regarding the respective interests of the principal and the attorney-in-fact.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4236 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: duty to keep records; when an accounting is required
citations.quote: The attorney-in-fact shall keep records of all transactions entered into by the attorney-in-fact on behalf of the principal. (b) The attorney-in-fact does not have a duty to make an account of transactions entered into on behalf of the principal, except in the following circumstances: (1) At any time requested by the principal. (2) Where the power of attorney requires the attorney-in-fact to account and specifies to whom the account is to be made. (3) On request by the conservator of the estate of the principal while the principal is living. (4) On request by the principal's personal representative or successor in interest after the death of the principal. (5) Pursuant to court order.

clauses.title: The Standard of Care an Agent Is Held To
clauses.body: In dealing with {{principalName}}'s property, an agent must observe the standard of care a prudent person would observe in dealing with someone else's property — a standard that is not limited by other statutes that otherwise restrict fiduciary investments. If {{agentName}} has, or was selected based on representations of, special skills or expertise, {{agentName}} is held to the higher standard of care that others with that same skill or expertise would observe. Where {{principalName}} names co-agents, one agent is not liable for another co-agent's actions unless that agent participates in, knowingly acquiesces in, or conceals the other agent's breach of fiduciary duty.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the standard of care an agent under a power of attorney is held to under one representative state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific power of attorney. The applicable standard, and any heightened-skill exception, vary by state.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4231 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: prudent-person standard of care; heightened standard for special skill/expertise
citations.quote: Except as provided in subdivision (b), in dealing with property of the principal, an attorney-in-fact shall observe the standard of care that would be observed by a prudent person dealing with property of another and is not limited by any other statute restricting investments by fiduciaries. (b) An attorney-in-fact who has special skills or expertise or was designated as an attorney-in-fact on the basis of representations of special skills or expertise shall observe the standard of care that would be observed by others with similar skills or expertise.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4202(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: no vicarious liability among co-agents absent participation
citations.quote: An attorney-in-fact is not liable for the actions of other attorneys-in-fact, unless the attorney-in-fact participates in, knowingly acquiesces in, or conceals a breach of fiduciary duty committed by another attorney-in-fact.

clauses.title: What a General Grant of Authority Actually Covers
clauses.body: When a statutory-form power of attorney grants authority over "real property transactions," California law construes that grant to empower the agent to buy, sell, lease, mortgage, exchange, manage, insure, and otherwise deal with an interest in real property or a right incident to it, including paying or contesting taxes and assessments and making repairs or alterations — unless the document itself limits or extends that authority. Similarly, a grant of authority over "banking and other financial institution transactions" empowers the agent to open, modify, and close accounts, use a safe deposit box, withdraw funds, endorse and negotiate checks and notes, borrow money and pledge personal property as security, and apply for letters of credit or credit cards, among other listed banking acts.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how a general grant of authority over a named subject (like real property or banking) is actually construed under one representative state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs the interpretation of a specific power of attorney. This construction specifically applies to the statutory-form power of attorney under this state's law; a custom-drafted document's language could be construed differently.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4451 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: scope of authority over real property transactions
citations.quote: In a statutory form power of attorney, the language granting power with respect to real property transactions empowers the agent to do all of the following: (a) Accept as a gift or as security for a loan, reject, demand, buy, lease, receive, or otherwise acquire, an interest in real property or a right incident to real property. (b) Sell, exchange, convey with or without covenants, quitclaim, release, surrender, mortgage, encumber, partition, consent to partitioning, subdivide, apply for zoning, rezoning, or other governmental permits, plat or consent to platting, develop, grant options concerning, lease, sublease, or otherwise dispose of, an interest in real property or a right incident to real property.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4455 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: scope of authority over banking transactions
citations.quote: In a statutory form power of attorney, the language granting power with respect to banking and other financial institution transactions empowers the agent to do all of the following: (a) Continue, modify, and terminate an account or other banking arrangement made by or on behalf of the principal. (b) Establish, modify, and terminate an account or other banking arrangement with a bank, trust company, savings and loan association, credit union, thrift company, industrial loan company, brokerage firm, or other financial institution selected by the agent. (c) Hire or close a safe deposit box or space in a vault.

clauses.title: Powers That Require Express, Specific Authorization
clauses.body: Even under a broad general grant of authority, an agent may perform certain acts only if the power of attorney expressly grants that specific authority. That defined list includes: creating, modifying, revoking, or terminating a trust; funding a trust the principal didn't create; making or revoking a gift of the principal's property; disclaiming or renouncing an interest in an estate, trust, or other fund; creating or changing survivorship interests in the principal's property; designating or changing a beneficiary designation on property, a benefit, or a contract right payable on the principal's death; and making a loan to the agent. Separately, no power of attorney — even with express, specific language — may authorize an agent to make, publish, declare, amend, or revoke {{principalName}}'s will.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a defined category of powers requires express, specific authorization in the document — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific power of attorney, and not a claim that this exact list matches every state's list of powers requiring express authorization.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4264 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: list of acts requiring express authorization in the document
citations.quote: An attorney-in-fact under a power of attorney may perform any of the following acts on behalf of the principal or with the property of the principal only if the power of attorney expressly grants that authority to the attorney-in-fact: (a) Create, modify, revoke, or terminate a trust, in whole or in part ... (c) Make or revoke a gift of the principal's property in trust or otherwise. (d) Exercise the right to reject, disclaim, release, or consent to a reduction in, or modification of, a share in, or payment from, an estate, trust, or other fund on behalf of the principal ... (e) Create or change survivorship interests in the principal's property or in property in which the principal may have an interest. (f) Designate or change the designation of beneficiaries to receive any property, benefit, or contract right on the principal's death. (g) Make a loan to the attorney-in-fact.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4265 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: categorical prohibition on will-making authority, regardless of express authorization
citations.quote: A power of attorney may not authorize an attorney-in-fact to make, publish, declare, amend, or revoke the principal's will.

clauses.title: How and When a Power of Attorney Is Revoked
clauses.body: {{principalName}} may revoke a power of attorney in accordance with any revocation procedure the document itself specifies, or simply by a writing — the writing method is available regardless of what the document says, and cannot be limited or taken away by the document's own terms. Separately, if {{principalName}} grants inconsistent authority to one or more agents across two or more powers of attorney, the authority granted in the later document controls to the extent the two are inconsistent; this rule, too, cannot be limited by the document.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how revocation and later-document conflicts work under one representative state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific power of attorney.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4151 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: revocation while the principal has capacity
citations.quote: A principal may revoke a power of attorney as follows: (1) In accordance with the terms of the power of attorney. (2) By a writing. This paragraph is not subject to limitation in the power of attorney.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4130 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: later power of attorney controls to the extent of inconsistency
citations.quote: If a principal grants inconsistent authority to one or more attorneys-in-fact in two or more powers of attorney, the authority granted last controls to the extent of the inconsistency. (b) This section is not subject to limitation in the power of attorney.

clauses.title: What Ends the Power of Attorney or an Agent's Authority
clauses.body: An agent's authority under a power of attorney terminates on any of several statutory events, including: fulfillment or extinction of the document's purpose; revocation; {{principalName}}'s death (except as to specific authority a statute permits to be exercised after death); removal or resignation of the agent; the agent's incapacity (a temporary incapacity only suspends authority during the incapacity itself); dissolution or annulment of a marriage between {{principalName}} and a spouse-agent; and the agent's death. Notably, {{principalName}}'s death does not, by itself, retroactively undo an agent's or a third party's actions taken in good faith without actual knowledge of the death — those actions still bind {{principalName}}'s successors in interest.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what events terminate a power of attorney or an agent's authority under one representative state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific power of attorney.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4152 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: statutory list of events terminating an agent's authority
citations.quote: the authority of an attorney-in-fact under a power of attorney is terminated by any of the following events: (1) In accordance with the terms of the power of attorney. (2) Extinction of the subject or fulfillment of the purpose of the power of attorney. (3) Revocation of the attorney-in-fact's authority, as provided in Section 4153. (4) Death of the principal, except as to specific authority permitted by statute to be exercised after the principal's death. (5) Removal of the attorney-in-fact. (6) Resignation of the attorney-in-fact. (7) Incapacity of the attorney-in-fact, except that a temporary incapacity suspends the attorney-in-fact's authority only during the period of the incapacity. (8) Dissolution or annulment of the marriage of the attorney-in-fact and principal, as provided in Section 4154. (9) Death of the attorney-in-fact.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4304(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: good-faith acts without knowledge of the principal's death remain binding
citations.quote: The death of a principal who has executed a power of attorney, whether durable or nondurable, does not revoke or terminate the agency as to the attorney-in-fact or a third person who, without actual knowledge of the principal's death, acts in good faith under the power of attorney. Any action so taken, unless otherwise invalid or unenforceable, binds the principal's successors in interest.

clauses.title: Co-Agents and Successor Agents
clauses.body: {{principalName}} may designate more than one agent. Absent contrary instructions in the document, authority granted to two or more agents is exercisable only by their unanimous action — but if one agent is unavailable due to absence, illness, or other temporary incapacity, or if a vacancy occurs, the remaining agent(s) may act alone where necessary to accomplish the document's purpose or avoid irreparable injury to {{principalName}}'s interests. {{principalName}} may also designate one or more successor agents — such as {{alternateAgentName}} — to act if a prior agent's authority terminates; a successor agent is not liable for a predecessor's actions.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the default rule for co-agents and successor agents under one representative state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific power of attorney. The unanimity default is a background rule the document can override.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4202 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: default unanimity rule for co-agents, and exceptions for vacancy/unavailability
citations.quote: A principal may designate more than one attorney-in-fact in one or more powers of attorney. (b) Authority granted to two or more attorneys-in-fact is exercisable only by their unanimous action. (c) If a vacancy occurs, the remaining attorneys-in-fact may exercise the authority conferred as if they are the only attorneys-in-fact. (d) If an attorney-in-fact is unavailable because of absence, illness, or other temporary incapacity, the other attorneys-in-fact may exercise the authority under the power of attorney as if they are the only attorneys-in-fact, where necessary to accomplish the purposes of the power of attorney or to avoid irreparable injury to the principal's interests.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4203 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: successor agents; no liability for a predecessor's acts
citations.quote: A principal may designate one or more successor attorneys-in-fact to act if the authority of a predecessor attorney-in-fact terminates. (b) The principal may grant authority to another person, designated by name, by office, or by function, including the initial and any successor attorneys-in-fact, to designate at any time one or more successor attorneys-in-fact. (c) A successor attorney-in-fact is not liable for the actions of the predecessor attorney-in-fact.

clauses.title: A Third Party's Duty to Accept — and Liability for Wrongful Refusal
clauses.body: A third party (such as a bank or title company) must accord an agent acting under a power of attorney the same rights and privileges the third party would accord {{principalName}} personally — though the third party is not required to honor the agent's authority or conduct business with the agent in circumstances where {{principalName}} personally could not require the third party to act. If an agent furnishes an affidavit stating that, at the time the agent exercised the power, the agent had no actual knowledge that the power of attorney or the agent's authority had been terminated, revoked, or ended by {{principalName}}'s death or incapacity, and a third party then refuses to accept the agent's exercise of authority referenced in that affidavit, the third party becomes liable for attorney's fees incurred in any proceeding needed to confirm the agent's authority — unless a court finds the third party believed in good faith that the agent was unqualified or was exceeding or misusing the granted authority.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a third party's duty to accept a power of attorney and a mechanism imposing liability for wrongful refusal under one representative state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific power of attorney. The fee-liability mechanism described here is specifically tied to a statutory affidavit procedure and its good-faith exception, not a general damages remedy for any refusal.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4300 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: third party's duty to treat the agent as it would treat the principal
citations.quote: A third person shall accord an attorney-in-fact acting pursuant to the provisions of a power of attorney the same rights and privileges that would be accorded the principal if the principal were personally present and seeking to act. However, a third person is not required to honor the attorney-in-fact's authority or conduct business with the attorney-in-fact if the principal cannot require the third person to act or conduct business in the same circumstances.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4306(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: attorney's-fee liability for refusing to accept an agent's authority after an affidavit is furnished, and its good-faith exception
citations.quote: If an attorney-in-fact furnishes an affidavit pursuant to Section 4305, whether voluntarily or on demand, a third person dealing with the attorney-in-fact who refuses to accept the exercise of the attorney-in-fact's authority referred to in the affidavit is liable for attorney's fees incurred in an action or proceeding necessary to confirm the attorney-in-fact's qualifications or authority, unless the court determines that the third person believed in good faith that the attorney-in-fact was not qualified or was attempting to exceed or improperly exercise the attorney-in-fact's authority.

clauses.title: Appointment of Agent
clauses.body: {{principalName}} appoints {{agentName}} as agent (attorney-in-fact) to act on {{principalName}}'s behalf as described in this document. If {{agentName}} is unable or unwilling to serve, or stops serving, {{principalName}} appoints {{alternateAgentName}} as successor agent.

clauses.title: Signature, Witness, and Notarization
clauses.body:
Signature of {{principalName}}: ☐ _________________________ Date: ☐ _________________________

Two-witness option (used only if this document is not notarized):
Witness 1 — Signature: ☐ _________________________ Printed name: ☐ _________________________ Date: ☐ _________________________
Witness 2 — Signature: ☐ _________________________ Printed name: ☐ _________________________ Date: ☐ _________________________

Notary acknowledgment option (used only if this document is not witnessed):
State of ☐ _________________________, County of ☐ _________________________
On ☐ _________________________, before me, personally appeared {{principalName}}, proved to me on the basis of satisfactory evidence to be the person whose name is subscribed to this instrument.
Notary signature: ☐ _________________________ Printed name: ☐ _________________________ Commission expires: ☐ _________________________

clauses.title: The Two Kinds of Health Care Directive
clauses.body: California law recognizes two distinct components of an advance health care directive, and a single document can contain either or both: an individual health care instruction — {{patientName}}'s own direct instructions about care — and a power of attorney for health care, which names {{agentName}} as agent to make health care decisions for {{patientName}}. A power of attorney for health care may also include individual health care instructions within the same document.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual statutory structure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4605 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: definition of advance health care directive as either component
citations.quote: “Advance health care directive” or “advance directive” means either an individual health care instruction or a power of attorney for health care.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4671(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: a power of attorney for health care may also include individual instructions
citations.quote: An adult having capacity may execute a power of attorney for health care, as provided in Article 2 (commencing with Section 4680). The power of attorney for health care may authorize the agent to make health care decisions and may also include individual health care instructions.

clauses.title: How This Directive Must Be Signed
clauses.body: For this power of attorney for health care to be legally sufficient, it must state the date it is executed, be signed by {{patientName}} (or by another adult in {{patientName}}'s presence and at {{patientName}}'s direction), and be either acknowledged before a notary public or signed by at least two qualified witnesses. Only one of those two methods — witnesses or notarization — is required, not both.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual execution requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 4673(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4673(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: legal sufficiency requirements for a written directive
citations.quote: A written advance health care directive is legally sufficient if all of the following requirements are satisfied: (1) The advance directive contains the date of its execution. (2) The advance directive is signed either by the patient or in the patient’s name by another adult in the patient’s presence and at the patient’s direction. (3) The advance directive is either acknowledged before a notary public or signed by at least two witnesses who satisfy the requirements of Sections 4674 and 4675.

clauses.title: Who Cannot Serve as a Witness
clauses.body: If this directive is signed by witnesses rather than notarized, none of the following may act as a witness: {{patientName}}'s health care provider or an employee of that provider, the operator or an employee of a community care facility, the operator or an employee of a residential care facility for the elderly, or {{agentName}} (or any other individual named as agent). Separately, at least one of the two witnesses must be a person who is neither related to {{patientName}} by blood, marriage, or adoption, nor entitled to any part of {{patientName}}'s estate on death under an existing will or by operation of law — that disinterested-witness requirement applies to only one of the two witnesses, not both.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual disqualification rules — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 4674) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4674(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: categorical witness disqualifications
citations.quote: None of the following persons may act as a witness: (1) The patient’s health care provider or an employee of the patient’s health care provider. (2) The operator or an employee of a community care facility. (3) The operator or an employee of a residential care facility for the elderly. (4) The agent, where the advance directive is a power of attorney for health care.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4674(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the one-of-two disinterested-witness rule
citations.quote: At least one of the witnesses shall be an individual who is neither related to the patient by blood, marriage, or adoption, nor entitled to any portion of the patient’s estate upon the patient’s death under a will existing when the advance directive is executed or by operation of law then existing.

clauses.title: Extra Witness Rule for Skilled Nursing Facility Patients
clauses.body: If {{patientName}} is a patient in a skilled nursing facility at the time this directive is signed, it is not effective unless a patient advocate or ombudsman designated by the California Department of Aging also signs it as a witness — either as one of the two witnesses or in addition to notarization.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of an additional, real safeguard that applies specifically to skilled nursing facility patients — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 4675(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4675(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: patient advocate/ombudsman witness requirement
citations.quote: If an individual is a patient in a skilled nursing facility when a written advance health care directive is executed, the advance directive is not effective unless a patient advocate or ombudsman, as may be designated by the Department of Aging for this purpose pursuant to any other applicable provision of law, signs the advance directive as a witness, either as one of two witnesses or in addition to notarization.

clauses.title: When the Agent's Authority Takes Effect
clauses.body: Unless this directive itself says otherwise, {{agentName}}'s authority to make health care decisions for {{patientName}} becomes effective only once a determination is made that {{patientName}} lacks the capacity to make their own health care decisions, and that authority ends if {{patientName}} is later determined to have recovered capacity. Unless the directive specifies otherwise, that determination is made by {{patientName}}'s primary physician.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual default timing rule and who makes the determination — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4682 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: default trigger for the agent's authority
citations.quote: Unless otherwise provided in a power of attorney for health care, the authority of an agent becomes effective only on a determination that the principal lacks capacity, and ceases to be effective on a determination that the principal has recovered capacity.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4658 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: who makes the capacity determination
citations.quote: Unless otherwise specified in a written advance health care directive, for the purposes of this division, a determination that a patient lacks or has recovered capacity, or that another condition exists that affects an individual health care instruction or the authority of an agent or surrogate, shall be made by the primary physician.

clauses.title: How the Agent Must Decide
clauses.body: {{agentName}} is required to make health care decisions for {{patientName}} in accordance with {{patientName}}'s individual health care instructions, if any, and {{patientName}}'s other wishes to the extent {{agentName}} knows them. Where those wishes are not known, {{agentName}} must decide based on {{agentName}}'s determination of {{patientName}}'s best interest, considering {{patientName}}'s personal values to the extent known.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual statutory decision-making standard imposed on a health care agent — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 4684); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4684 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the agent's decision-making standard
citations.quote: An agent shall make a health care decision in accordance with the principal’s individual health care instructions, if any, and other wishes to the extent known to the agent. Otherwise, the agent shall make the decision in accordance with the agent’s determination of the principal’s best interest. In determining the principal’s best interest, the agent shall consider the principal’s personal values to the extent known to the agent.

clauses.title: What the Agent Can and Cannot Decide
clauses.body: Unless this directive limits it, {{agentName}}'s authority to make health care decisions for {{patientName}} is as broad as {{patientName}}'s own authority would be — including consenting to or refusing any care, treatment, service, or procedure, and selecting or discharging health care providers and institutions. State law nonetheless withholds some decisions entirely, regardless of what this directive says: it does not authorize consent, on {{patientName}}'s behalf, to commitment to or placement in a mental health treatment facility, convulsive treatment, psychosurgery, sterilization, or abortion.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of both the actual breadth of a health care agent's default authority and a real, specific statutory carve-out from it — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4683(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the breadth of the agent's default authority
citations.quote: An agent designated in the power of attorney may make health care decisions for the principal to the same extent the principal could make health care decisions if the principal had the capacity to do so.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4652 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the statutory carve-out from any consent authority
citations.quote: This division does not authorize consent to any of the following on behalf of a patient: (a) Commitment to or placement in a mental health treatment facility. (b) Convulsive treatment (as defined in Section 5325 of the Welfare and Institutions Code). (c) Psychosurgery (as defined in Section 5325 of the Welfare and Institutions Code). (d) Sterilization. (e) Abortion.

clauses.title: Access to Medical Records
clauses.body: Unless this directive specifies otherwise, {{agentName}} — once authorized to make health care decisions for {{patientName}} — has the same right {{patientName}} has to request, receive, examine, copy, and consent to the disclosure of {{patientName}}'s medical and other health care information. Separately, under the federal HIPAA Privacy Rule, a health care provider that is a covered entity must treat a person who has authority under state law to make health care decisions for an adult patient as that patient's personal representative for purposes of accessing the patient's protected health information.
clauses.gap: The state-law records-access right and the federal HIPAA personal-representative rule are two independent sources addressing different bodies of law: the California statute is used as real evidence of a state-law records-access right for whoever is authorized to decide — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive — while the cited HIPAA provision is a real, separately sourced federal regulation about medical-record privacy and access, not the source of an agent's authority to make health care decisions in the first place; HIPAA does not create or govern that decision-making authority.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4678 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the authorized decision-maker's records-access right
citations.quote: Unless otherwise specified in an advance health care directive, a person then authorized to make health care decisions for a patient has the same rights as the patient to request, receive, examine, copy, and consent to the disclosure of medical or any other health care information.

citations.case: 45 C.F.R. § 164.502(g)(1)-(2) (eCFR text, HIPAA Privacy Rule)
citations.cite: the federal personal-representative standard, tied to state health-care-decision authority
citations.quote: As specified in this paragraph, a covered entity must, except as provided in paragraphs (g)(3) and (g)(5) of this section, treat a personal representative as the individual for purposes of this subchapter. (2) If under applicable law a person has authority to act on behalf of an individual who is an adult or an emancipated minor in making decisions related to health care, a covered entity must treat such person as a personal representative under this subchapter, with respect to protected health information relevant to such personal representation.

clauses.title: How This Directive Can Be Revoked
clauses.body: While having capacity, {{patientName}} may revoke the designation of {{agentName}} as agent only by a signed writing or by personally informing the supervising health care provider — not by any other method. Any other part of this directive can be revoked at any time and in any manner that communicates an intent to revoke, without needing a signed writing.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual, non-uniform revocation mechanics — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 4695) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4695(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the stricter method for revoking an agent designation
citations.quote: A patient having capacity may revoke the designation of an agent only by a signed writing or by personally informing the supervising health care provider.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4695(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the looser method for revoking everything else
citations.quote: A patient having capacity may revoke all or part of an advance health care directive, other than the designation of an agent, at any time and in any manner that communicates an intent to revoke.

clauses.title: What a Later Divorce Does to an Agent Designation
clauses.body: If {{agentName}} is {{patientName}}'s spouse and, after this directive is executed, {{patientName}}'s marriage to {{agentName}} is dissolved or annulled, the designation of {{agentName}} as agent is automatically revoked by that dissolution or annulment alone. If {{patientName}} later remarries {{agentName}}, the revoked designation is automatically revived.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a real, automatic default specific to this state's Health Care Decisions Law — not an assumption that it mirrors this state's separate rule for wills, and not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 4697) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4697(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: automatic revocation of a spouse-agent designation on divorce
citations.quote: If after executing a power of attorney for health care the principal’s marriage to the agent is dissolved or annulled, the principal’s designation of the former spouse as an agent to make health care decisions for the principal is revoked.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4697(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: automatic revival on remarriage
citations.quote: If the agent’s authority is revoked solely by subdivision (a), it is revived by the principal’s remarriage to the agent.

clauses.title: A Health Care Provider's Duty to Comply or Transfer
clauses.body: Except for the reasons-of-conscience exception described below, a health care provider or health care institution treating {{patientName}} must comply with {{patientName}}'s individual health care instructions and with any health care decision made by {{agentName}} or another person then authorized to decide for {{patientName}}, to the same extent as if {{patientName}} had made the decision personally. A health care provider may decline for reasons of conscience, and a health care institution may decline based on a conscience-based policy that was timely communicated to {{patientName}} or {{agentName}}; in either case, the provider or institution must promptly say so, make all reasonable efforts to transfer {{patientName}} to a provider or institution willing to comply, and continue care — including pain relief and other palliative care — until the transfer happens or appears impossible.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual compliance duty and its real conscience-based exception — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4733 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the compliance duty
citations.quote: Except as provided in Sections 4734 and 4735, a health care provider or health care institution providing care to a patient shall do the following: (a) Comply with an individual health care instruction of the patient and with a reasonable interpretation of that instruction made by a person then authorized to make health care decisions for the patient. (b) Comply with a health care decision for the patient made by a person then authorized to make health care decisions for the patient to the same extent as if the decision had been made by the patient while having capacity.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4736 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the notify-and-transfer duty when a provider declines
citations.quote: A health care provider or health care institution that declines to comply with an individual health care instruction or health care decision shall do all of the following: (a) Promptly so inform the patient, if possible, and any person then authorized to make health care decisions for the patient. (b) Unless the patient or person then authorized to make health care decisions for the patient refuses assistance, immediately make all reasonable efforts to assist in the transfer of the patient to another health care provider or institution that is willing to comply with the instruction or decision. (c) Provide continuing care to the patient until a transfer can be accomplished or until it appears that a transfer cannot be accomplished. In all cases, appropriate pain relief and other palliative care shall be continued.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4734 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the reasons-of-conscience exception
citations.quote: (a) A health care provider may decline to comply with an individual health care instruction or health care decision for reasons of conscience. (b) A health care institution may decline to comply with an individual health care instruction or health care decision if the instruction or decision is contrary to a policy of the institution that is expressly based on reasons of conscience and if the policy was timely communicated to the patient or to a person then authorized to make health care decisions for the patient.

clauses.title: Good-Faith Immunity for Providers and Agents
clauses.body: A health care provider or health care institution that acts in good faith, consistent with generally accepted health care standards, is not subject to civil or criminal liability or professional discipline for complying with a health care decision it believes in good faith was made by someone with authority to make it. {{agentName}}, acting as agent, is likewise not subject to civil or criminal liability or professional discipline for health care decisions made in good faith.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual immunity and its real limit — the protection runs only to good-faith conduct, and the same statute separately imposes civil damages, and in some circumstances criminal homicide liability, on a provider, agent, or anyone else who acts in bad faith, such as by intentionally falsifying, concealing, or fraudulently inducing a directive — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4740 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: provider/institution good-faith immunity
