citations.quote: A health care provider or health care institution acting in good faith and in accordance with generally accepted health care standards applicable to the health care provider or institution is not subject to civil or criminal liability or to discipline for unprofessional conduct for any actions in compliance with this division, including, but not limited to, any of the following conduct: (a) Complying with a health care decision of a person that the health care provider or health care institution believes in good faith has the authority to make a health care decision for a patient, including a decision to withhold or withdraw health care.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4741 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: agent/surrogate good-faith immunity
citations.quote: A person acting as agent or surrogate under this part is not subject to civil or criminal liability or to discipline for unprofessional conduct for health care decisions made in good faith.

clauses.title: California's Optional Statutory Form
clauses.body: California Probate Code provides an optional statutory form for an advance health care directive. Using that state-provided form is not required — any writing that satisfies the execution requirements described above is legally sufficient, and an individual may complete or modify all or any part of the statutory form.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a state-provided model form actually exists and is optional — not a recommendation about which format to use, and not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 4700); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4700 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the optional statutory form
citations.quote: The form provided in Section 4701 may, but need not, be used to create an advance health care directive. The other sections of this division govern the effect of the form or any other writing used to create an advance health care directive. An individual may complete or modify all or any part of the form in Section 4701.

clauses.title: Declaration and Appointment of Agent
clauses.body: I, {{patientName}}, being an adult of sound mind, make this Advance Health Care Directive to make known my wishes regarding my own health care and to designate an agent to make health care decisions for me as described in this document. I revoke any prior advance health care directive or power of attorney for health care I have made. I designate {{agentName}} as my agent to make health care decisions for me. If {{agentName}} is unable, unwilling, or not reasonably available to act, I designate {{alternateAgentName}} as my alternate agent.

clauses.title: Specific Wishes for End-of-Life Care
clauses.body: Regarding treatment intended to prolong my life: ☐ {{lifeProlongingWishes}}. Regarding relief from pain or discomfort: ☐ {{painReliefWishes}}. Additional instructions regarding my physical or mental health care: ☐ {{additionalHealthCareWishes}}.

clauses.title: Signatures
clauses.body:
Signature of {{patientName}}: ☐ _________________________ Date: ☐ _________________________

This directive is signed either before a notary public or in the presence of two qualified witnesses, whose acknowledgment or signatures and declarations appear on an attached page.

clauses.title: How a Trust Is Created
clauses.body: California law recognizes several distinct methods of creating a trust: a declaration by the owner of property that the owner holds the property as trustee; a transfer of property by the owner, during the owner's lifetime, to another person as trustee; a transfer of property by will or other instrument taking effect at the owner's death; the exercise of a power of appointment in favor of a trustee; or an enforceable promise to create a trust. This trust is created by {{settlorName}}'s lifetime transfer of property to {{trusteeName}} as trustee.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual methods California recognizes for creating a trust — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. A declaration or transfer that satisfies one of these methods still has to satisfy the separate requirements for a valid trust — settlor intent, a legal purpose, and (except for a charitable trust) an ascertainable beneficiary — addressed elsewhere in this document. This is a single statutory section (§ 15200); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15200 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the statutory methods of creating a trust
citations.quote: Subject to other provisions of this chapter, a trust may be created by any of the following methods: (a) A declaration by the owner of property that the owner holds the property as trustee. (b) A transfer of property by the owner during the owner's lifetime to another person as trustee. (c) A transfer of property by the owner, by will or by other instrument taking effect upon the death of the owner, to another person as trustee. (d) An exercise of a power of appointment to another person as trustee. (e) An enforceable promise to create a trust.

clauses.title: Requirements for a Valid Trust
clauses.body: Beyond using one of the statutory methods of creation, a trust is valid only if {{settlorName}} properly manifests an intention to create a trust, the trust is created for a purpose that is not illegal or against public policy, and — unless the trust is a valid charitable trust — there is a beneficiary who is ascertainable with reasonable certainty, or sufficiently described that it can be determined whether a given person meets the description, or whose selection is left to the trustee's or another person's discretion under a stated standard.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual requirements for a valid trust — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. These three requirements — intent, lawful purpose, and an ascertainable beneficiary — are independent of the funding requirements addressed elsewhere in this document; a trust can satisfy all three and still fail to hold property that was never actually transferred into it.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15201 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the settlor's-intent requirement
citations.quote: A trust is created only if the settlor properly manifests an intention to create a trust.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15203 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the lawful-purpose requirement
citations.quote: A trust may be created for any purpose that is not illegal or against public policy.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15205 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the ascertainable-beneficiary requirement and charitable-trust exception
citations.quote: (a) A trust, other than a charitable trust, is created only if there is a beneficiary. (b) The requirement of subdivision (a) is satisfied if the trust instrument provides for either of the following: (1) A beneficiary or class of beneficiaries that is ascertainable with reasonable certainty or that is sufficiently described so it can be determined that some person meets the description or is within the class. (2) A grant of a power to the trustee or some other person to select the beneficiaries based on a standard or in the discretion of the trustee or other person.

clauses.title: Personal Property vs. Real Property — Different Formality Requirements
clauses.body: A trust of personal property carries no special formality requirement beyond what the law otherwise requires for the underlying transaction — an oral trust of personal property is legally possible, though its existence and terms can be established only by clear and convincing evidence, and the settlor's oral declaration alone is not enough. A trust relating to real property is held to a stricter standard: it isn't valid unless evidenced by a written instrument signed by the trustee (or the trustee's authorized agent), a written instrument conveying the property signed by the settlor (or the settlor's authorized agent), or by operation of law.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a real, easy-to-miss distinction — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This distinction matters beyond formality: a trust holds only the property actually transferred into it in a legally effective way, and real property that was never conveyed to the trustee by a qualifying written instrument remains outside the trust regardless of what the trust instrument says about it — meaning it stays subject to probate at the settlor's death rather than passing under the trust.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15206 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the written-instrument requirement for a trust of real property
citations.quote: A trust in relation to real property is not valid unless evidenced by one of the following methods: (a) By a written instrument signed by the trustee, or by the trustee's agent if authorized in writing to do so. (b) By a written instrument conveying the trust property signed by the settlor, or by the settlor's agent if authorized in writing to do so. (c) By operation of law.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15207(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: an oral trust of personal property is legally possible
citations.quote: (a) The existence and terms of an oral trust of personal property may be established only by clear and convincing evidence. (b) The oral declaration of the settlor, standing alone, is not sufficient evidence of the creation of a trust of personal property.

clauses.title: Revocability — the Default Rule and How to Revoke
clauses.body: Unless {{trustName}} is expressly made irrevocable by its own terms, it is revocable by {{settlorName}} — revocability, not irrevocability, is the default under California law for a trust the settlor creates while domiciled in California, executed in California, or that states California law governs. {{settlorName}} can revoke the trust, in whole or in part, by following any revocation method the trust instrument itself provides, or — if the trust instrument doesn't make its own method the exclusive one — by a signed writing, other than a will, delivered to {{trusteeName}} during {{settlorName}}'s lifetime.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual default rule and revocation methods — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. Where more than one person contributed property to the same trust, or where someone other than the settlor holds a power of revocation, additional statutory provisions address revocation of just that person's contributed share; those situations aren't addressed here.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15400 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: revocability is the statutory default
citations.quote: Unless a trust is expressly made irrevocable by the trust instrument, the trust is revocable by the settlor. This section applies only where the settlor is domiciled in this state when the trust is created, where the trust instrument is executed in this state, or where the trust instrument provides that the law of this state governs the trust.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15401(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the statutory methods of revocation
citations.quote: (a) A trust that is revocable by the settlor or any other person may be revoked in whole or in part by any of the following methods: (1) By compliance with any method of revocation provided in the trust instrument. (2) By a writing, other than a will, signed by the settlor or any other person holding the power of revocation and delivered to the trustee during the lifetime of the settlor or the person holding the power of revocation. If the trust instrument explicitly makes the method of revocation provided in the trust instrument the exclusive method of revocation, the trust may not be revoked pursuant to this paragraph.

clauses.title: Trustee's Duty of Loyalty and Duty to Keep Trust Property Separate
clauses.body: {{trusteeName}}, acting as trustee, has a duty to administer the trust solely in the interest of the beneficiaries, and a separate duty to keep trust property separate from {{trusteeName}}'s own property and to see that trust property is identified as property of the trust.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of two genuine, specific fiduciary duties among several a trustee owes — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust, and not a complete list of a trustee's duties. A trustee who also administers a second trust may sell or exchange property between the two trusts without violating the duty of loyalty if the exchange is fair to both trusts' beneficiaries and both sets of beneficiaries are notified of the material facts — a narrow statutory exception to the general rule stated above.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16002(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the trustee's duty of loyalty
citations.quote: (a) The trustee has a duty to administer the trust solely in the interest of the beneficiaries.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16009 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the trustee's duty to keep trust property separate
citations.quote: The trustee has a duty to do the following: (a) To keep the trust property separate from other property not subject to the trust. (b) To see that the trust property is designated as property of the trust.

clauses.title: Whose Interests the Trustee Serves While the Trust Is Revocable
clauses.body: For as long as the trust remains revocable and {{settlorName}} (or whoever else holds the power to revoke) is competent, the rights the law otherwise gives to trust beneficiaries belong instead to the person holding the power to revoke, and the trustee's duties run to that person — not to the beneficiaries named in the trust. Where a beneficiary's consent would otherwise be required or permitted for some action, it's the person holding the power to revoke, not the beneficiary, who has the power to give or withhold that consent, during that same period.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuinely counter-intuitive default — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. If, while the trust is still revocable, no one holding the power to revoke remains competent, the statute shifts the trustee's accounting and disclosure duties to the beneficiaries who would receive income or principal if the settlor had died at that point — the rule addressed in this clause is specifically about the period when someone with the power to revoke is still competent.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15800(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: trustee's duties run to the person holding the power to revoke
citations.quote: (a) Except to the extent that the trust instrument otherwise provides or where the joint action of the settlor and all beneficiaries is required, during the time that a trust is revocable and at least one person holding the power to revoke the trust, in whole or in part, is competent, the following shall apply: (1) The person holding the power to revoke, and not the beneficiary, has the rights afforded beneficiaries under this division. (2) The duties of the trustee are owed to the person holding the power to revoke.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15801(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: consent rights belong to the person holding the power to revoke
citations.quote: (a) In any case where the consent of a beneficiary may be given or is required to be given before an action may be taken, during the time that a trust is revocable and the person holding the power to revoke the trust is competent, the person holding the power to revoke, and not the beneficiary, has the power to consent or withhold consent.

clauses.title: Filling a Vacancy in the Office of Trustee
clauses.body: If {{trustName}} has no trustee — including because {{trusteeName}} has died or become incapacitated — the vacancy is filled first by whatever practical method or named successor the trust instrument itself provides. Only if the trust instrument doesn't fill the vacancy that way does the law step in: a trust company that agrees to accept the trust may fill the vacancy with the agreement of all adult beneficiaries currently entitled to income or principal, or a court may appoint a trustee on petition of an interested person or a person named as trustee in the trust instrument.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the statutory fallback for filling a vacant trusteeship — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This is the mechanism a revocable living trust relies on to keep the trust administered without a court-supervised conservatorship if the settlor becomes incapacitated or dies — but it works automatically only if the trust instrument's own successor-trustee provision is functional; where it fails or is silent, the statutory fallback above requires either beneficiary agreement or a court petition, neither of which is automatic. This is a single statutory section (§ 15660); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15660(b)-(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: filling a vacancy in the office of trustee
citations.quote: (b) If the trust instrument provides a practical method of appointing a trustee or names the person to fill the vacancy, the vacancy shall be filled as provided in the trust instrument. (c) If the vacancy in the office of trustee is not filled as provided in subdivision (b), the vacancy may be filled by a trust company that has agreed to accept the trust on agreement of all adult beneficiaries who are receiving or are entitled to receive income under the trust or to receive a distribution of principal if the trust were terminated at the time the agreement is made. If a beneficiary has a conservator, the conservator may agree to the successor trustee on behalf of the conservatee without obtaining court approval. Without limiting the power of the beneficiary to agree to the successor trustee, if the beneficiary has designated an attorney in fact who has the power under the power of attorney to agree to the successor trustee, the attorney in fact may agree to the successor trustee. (d) If the vacancy in the office of trustee is not filled as provided in subdivision (b) or (c), on petition of any interested person or any person named as trustee in the trust instrument, the court may, in its discretion, appoint a trustee to fill the vacancy.

clauses.title: Consideration Is Not Required
clauses.body: Unlike a contract, a trust does not require consideration to be valid — {{settlorName}} can create a trust as a gift, with nothing given in exchange. A promise to create a trust in the future is treated differently: that promise is enforceable only if it independently satisfies the requirements for an enforceable contract, consideration included.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a real, easy-to-miss statutory rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This is a single statutory section (§ 15208); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15208 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: consideration is not required to create a trust
citations.quote: Consideration is not required to create a trust, but a promise to create a trust in the future is enforceable only if the requirements for an enforceable contract are satisfied.

clauses.title: Trustee's Duty to Account — and Its Limits While the Trust Is Revocable
clauses.body: {{trusteeName}}, acting as trustee, has a duty to account at least annually, at the trust's termination, and upon any change of trustee, to each beneficiary currently entitled — or authorized in the trustee's discretion — to receive income or principal. That duty doesn't run to beneficiaries generally while the trust is revocable and someone holding the power to revoke remains competent — during that period, as stated elsewhere in this document, the accounting duty runs to the person holding the power to revoke instead.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the accounting duty and how the statute itself reconciles it with the revocable-trust settlor's-interest rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. Additional statutory exceptions to the accounting duty exist beyond the revocable-trust exception addressed here, including a trust instrument's waiver of accounting (subject to its own limits) and a beneficiary's individual written waiver.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16062(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the trustee's duty to account
citations.quote: (a) Except as otherwise provided in this section and in Section 16064, the trustee shall account at least annually, at the termination of the trust, and upon a change of trustee, to each beneficiary to whom income or principal is required or authorized in the trustee's discretion to be currently distributed.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16069(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the accounting duty doesn't run to beneficiaries while the trust is revocable
citations.quote: (a) The trustee is not required to account to the beneficiary, provide the terms of the trust to a beneficiary, or provide requested information to the beneficiary pursuant to Section 16061, in any of the following circumstances: (1) In the case of a beneficiary of a revocable trust, as provided in subdivision (a) of Section 15800, for the period when the trust may be revoked.

clauses.title: Relationship to a Pour-Over Will
clauses.body: California law allows a will to devise property to the trustee of a trust that the testator established, or is establishing, elsewhere — a trust identified in the will, with its terms set out in a written instrument other than the will itself, executed before, at the same time as, or within 60 days after the will. Property devised this way isn't treated as held under a separate trust created by the will; it simply becomes part of the trust it's given to, administered under that trust's own terms, and the devise isn't invalidated merely because the trust is amendable or revocable.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual statutory basis for a pour-over provision — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust or will. This is the mechanism connecting a companion will to a living trust: property the settlor never transferred into the trust during life, but that the will directs to the trust at death, still has to pass through probate to get there — a pour-over provision routes probate property into the trust rather than avoiding probate for that property. If the trust is revoked or terminated before the testator's death, the devise lapses unless the will itself says otherwise. This is a single statutory section (§ 6300); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6300(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: a will may devise property to a trustee (the pour-over statute)
citations.quote: (a) A devise, the validity of which is determinable by the law of this state, may be made by a will to the trustee of a trust established or to be established by the testator, by the testator and some other person, or by some other person (including a funded or unfunded life insurance trust, although the settlor has reserved any or all rights of ownership of the insurance contracts) if the trust is identified in the testator's will and its terms are set forth in a written instrument (other than a will) executed before, concurrently with, or within 60 days after the execution of the testator's will or in the valid last will of a person who has predeceased the testator (regardless of the existence, size, or character of the trust property). The devise is not invalid because the trust is amendable or revocable, or both, or because the trust was amended after the execution of the will or after the death of the testator. (b) Unless the testator's will provides otherwise, the property so devised (1) is not deemed to be held under a testamentary trust of the testator but becomes a part of the trust to which it is given and (2) shall be administered and disposed of in accordance with the provisions of the instrument or will setting forth the terms of the trust, including any amendments thereto made before or after the death of the testator (regardless of whether made before or after the execution of the testator's will).

clauses.title: Declaration
clauses.body: I, {{settlorName}}, of {{settlorCounty}} County, California, as settlor, declare that I am creating the {{trustName}}, and that I am transferring the property described in the attached schedule to {{trusteeName}}, as initial trustee, to hold, administer, and distribute according to the terms of this trust. Upon the death, resignation, or incapacity of {{trusteeName}}, {{successorTrusteeName}} shall serve as successor trustee.

clauses.title: Authorization Required to Use or Disclose Protected Health Information
clauses.body: Under the HIPAA Privacy Rule, a covered entity (a health care provider, health plan, or health care clearinghouse) may not use or disclose {{patientName}}'s protected health information without a valid authorization, except as otherwise permitted or required by the Privacy Rule. This document is {{patientName}}'s written authorization for {{authorizedRecipientName}} to receive the protected health information described below, consistent with the terms stated here.
clauses.gap: This is a single regulatory subsection (45 C.F.R. § 164.508); no additional independent source was found for this. This is a federal regulation that applies nationwide — unlike the state-law documents elsewhere in this project's Estate Planning category, this authorization's legal basis does not vary by state.

citations.cite: authorization required: general rule
citations.quote: Except as otherwise permitted or required by this subchapter, a covered entity may not use or disclose protected health information without an authorization that is valid under this section. When a covered entity obtains or receives a valid authorization for its use or disclosure of protected health information, such use or disclosure must be consistent with such authorization.

clauses.title: Required Core Elements of a Valid Authorization
clauses.body: A valid authorization under the Privacy Rule must contain: a specific and meaningful description of the information to be used or disclosed; the identity of the person(s) authorized to make the disclosure; the identity of {{authorizedRecipientName}} as the person to whom disclosure may be made; a description of the purpose of the disclosure; an expiration date or expiration event ({{expirationDate}}); and the signature of {{patientName}} and the date signed.
clauses.gap: This is a single regulatory subsection (45 C.F.R. § 164.508); no additional independent source was found for this. This is a federal regulation that applies nationwide — unlike the state-law documents elsewhere in this project's Estate Planning category, this authorization's legal basis does not vary by state.

citations.cite: core elements
citations.quote: A valid authorization under this section must contain at least the following elements: (i) A description of the information to be used or disclosed that identifies the information in a specific and meaningful fashion. (ii) The name or other specific identification of the person(s), or class of persons, authorized to make the requested use or disclosure. (iii) The name or other specific identification of the person(s), or class of persons, to whom the covered entity may make the requested use or disclosure. (iv) A description of each purpose of the requested use or disclosure. The statement "at the request of the individual" is a sufficient description of the purpose when an individual initiates the authorization and does not, or elects not to, provide a statement of the purpose. (v) An expiration date or an expiration event that relates to the individual or the purpose of the use or disclosure. (vi) Signature of the individual and date. If the authorization is signed by a personal representative of the individual, a description of such representative's authority to act for the individual must also be provided.

clauses.title: Required Notice Statements Within an Authorization
clauses.body: In addition to the core elements above, the Privacy Rule requires that an authorization state: that {{patientName}} has the right to revoke this authorization in writing, subject to stated exceptions; whether treatment, payment, enrollment, or eligibility for benefits may be conditioned on signing this authorization; and that information disclosed under this authorization may be subject to redisclosure by {{authorizedRecipientName}} and, once redisclosed, may no longer be protected by the Privacy Rule.
clauses.gap: This is a single regulatory subsection (45 C.F.R. § 164.508); no additional independent source was found for this. This is a federal regulation that applies nationwide — unlike the state-law documents elsewhere in this project's Estate Planning category, this authorization's legal basis does not vary by state.

citations.cite: required statements
citations.quote: In addition to the core elements, the authorization must contain statements adequate to place the individual on notice of all of the following: (i) The individual's right to revoke the authorization in writing... (ii) The ability or inability to condition treatment, payment, enrollment or eligibility for benefits on the authorization... (iii) The potential for information disclosed pursuant to the authorization to be subject to redisclosure by the recipient and no longer be protected by this subpart.

clauses.title: Right to Revoke an Authorization
clauses.body: {{patientName}} may revoke this authorization in writing at any time, except to the extent a covered entity has already taken action in reliance on it, or, if this authorization was obtained as a condition of obtaining insurance coverage, to the extent other law gives the insurer a right to contest a claim under the policy.
clauses.gap: This is a single regulatory subsection (45 C.F.R. § 164.508); no additional independent source was found for this. This is a federal regulation that applies nationwide — unlike the state-law documents elsewhere in this project's Estate Planning category, this authorization's legal basis does not vary by state.

citations.cite: revocation of authorizations
citations.quote: An individual may revoke an authorization provided under this section at any time, provided that the revocation is in writing, except to the extent that: (i) The covered entity has taken action in reliance thereon; or (ii) If the authorization was obtained as a condition of obtaining insurance coverage, other law provides the insurer with the right to contest a claim under the policy or the policy itself.

clauses.title: What Makes an Authorization Invalid
clauses.body: Under the Privacy Rule, a signed authorization is not valid if: its stated expiration date has passed or its expiration event is known to a covered entity to have occurred; it was not filled out completely as to a required element; a covered entity knows it has been revoked; it violates the compound-authorization rules that apply, where relevant; or a covered entity knows material information in it to be false.
clauses.gap: This is a single regulatory subsection (45 C.F.R. § 164.508); no additional independent source was found for this. This is a federal regulation that applies nationwide — unlike the state-law documents elsewhere in this project's Estate Planning category, this authorization's legal basis does not vary by state.

citations.cite: defective authorizations
citations.quote: An authorization is not valid, if the document submitted has any of the following defects: (i) The expiration date has passed or the expiration event is known by the covered entity to have occurred; (ii) The authorization has not been filled out completely, with respect to an element described by paragraph (c) of this section, if applicable; (iii) The authorization is known by the covered entity to have been revoked; (iv) The authorization violates paragraph (b)(3) or (4) of this section, if applicable; (v) Any material information in the authorization is known by the covered entity to be false.

clauses.title: How This Authorization Differs From Treatment-Related Disclosures
clauses.body: Separately from this authorization, the Privacy Rule permits a covered entity to use or disclose protected health information for its own treatment, payment, and health care operations without an authorization, and permits a covered entity to obtain a patient's optional consent for that separate purpose. This authorization is a different instrument: it is the specific mechanism the Privacy Rule requires before protected health information can be used or disclosed for purposes outside that treatment-payment-operations category, or in the manner and to the recipient {{patientName}} specifies here.
clauses.gap: This is a federal regulation that applies nationwide — unlike the state-law documents elsewhere in this project's Estate Planning category, this authorization's legal basis does not vary by state.

citations.cite: authorization required: general rule
citations.quote: Except as otherwise permitted or required by this subchapter, a covered entity may not use or disclose protected health information without an authorization that is valid under this section.

citations.cite: uses and disclosures to carry out treatment, payment, or health care operations
citations.quote: a covered entity may use or disclose protected health information for treatment, payment, or health care operations as set forth in paragraph (c) of this section, provided that such use or disclosure is consistent with other applicable requirements of this subpart... A covered entity may obtain consent of the individual to use or disclose protected health information to carry out treatment, payment, or health care operations. Consent, under paragraph (b) of this section, shall not be effective to permit a use or disclosure of protected health information when an authorization, under § 164.508, is required or when another condition must be met for such use or disclosure to be permissible under this subpart.

clauses.title: A Note on California's Separate Medical-Privacy Statute
clauses.body: Independent of HIPAA, California's Confidentiality of Medical Information Act separately restricts a California health care provider's disclosure of medical information about {{patientName}} without first obtaining an authorization, subject to statutory exceptions. This state statute exists alongside, and is not part of, the federal HIPAA authorization requirements described above.
clauses.gap: This is a single state-law citation (Cal. Civ. Code § 56.10(a)); no additional independent source was found for this. Unlike the federal HIPAA baseline elsewhere in this clause set, this specific point of California law does not apply nationwide — it supplements, rather than substitutes for, the federal Privacy Rule requirements above.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 56.10(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Confidentiality of Medical Information Act — disclosure by providers
citations.quote: A provider of health care, health care service plan, or contractor shall not disclose medical information regarding a patient of the provider of health care or an enrollee or subscriber of a health care service plan without first obtaining an authorization, except as provided in subdivision (b) or (c).
